subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.

speechtext:
Sir GEORGE FOSTER moved the second reading of Bill No. 83, relating to the Honorary Advisory Council for Scientific and Industrial Research.
He said: , The outbreak of the war brought very forcibly home to the attention of most great countries of the world, particularly those on the Allied side of the contest, the march in advance that Germany had made in industrial and economic matters, which had made her the happy possessor of the basic raw materials in a great many of the different quarters of the globe, and had also transferred to her, in the process of years, practical monopolies in many of the key industries and basic industries of the world. So it happened that, after the war broke out, Great Britain especially found herself deprived of many processes which had been initiated, so to speak, in Great Britain itself by way of invention and primary development, but which had afterwards been gradually taken over by the German people and, under their peculiar and thorough methods, had come to be, as I have said, virtual monopolies; that is, Germany practically controlled the supply of the world and became the purveyor of these much needed and very valuable processes to the Test of the world. These matters were brought practically to the attention of the different Governments, and from that time France, Great Britain, Italy, the United States of America, Australia and Canada to a certain extent, have been practically alive to the situation and have been developing measures by which in the future they tshall not be dependent for those basic materials and basic processes upon alien or foreign countries. The British Government took the matter up and appointed., in July, 1915, a committee of the Privy Council, consisting of six official and three unofficial members, who should have, in general, charge of the encouragement and promotion of scientific and industrial research. This [DOT]committee of the Privy Council appointed a Council on Scientific and Industrial Research, advisory to the committee of the Privy Council. Sir William McCormick
presides over this council, and associated with him are seven other -members, eminent practical scientists of Great Britain. That Advisory Council undertook to make certain examinations, to. find out certain information, and to make practically available, so far as it was able to do so, the agencies and facilities for scientific and industrial research which already existed in Great Britain, .and, to co-ordinate as far as possible, the efforts of these dislocated and independent .agencies for research, and, in general, to stimulate the desire for and promote the development of industrial .and scientific research. The committee of the Privy Council were responsible to the Treasury Board for any moneys which would be placed .at their disposal, and they rely upon the Advisory Council for examination, anforma-ition, .advice 'and counsel. Within .a late period, at the end of last year, I think, or near the end of last year, after the Advisory Council bad been .at work for nearly ia year, and had made their .prelimimary survey, the British Government granted a charter to the subcommittee of the Council, forming it into an Imperial trust, .and they [DOT]have placed at the disposal of that subcommittee of the Privy Council about .a million pounds sterling for the various purposes which they .had in view. This Imperial Trust is .also -allowed itio take bequests that may be made from any quarter whatsoever, and -to manage the funds made u.p of appropriations by the Government .and of bequests from individuals or corporations. This scheme was at first entirely confined to the United Kingdom, but it soon became apparent that it might, with advantage, be extended in the scope of its work, and as a consequence communications were bad with the Overseas Dominions, and the proposal was made that in such way -as might be deemed best by the Overseas Dominions, co-operation in such research work should he had, .and as a result of such co-operation, agencies, were appointed or arranged for in the Overseas Dominions, through which there might be communication between and co-operation of effort, and the distribution of the results .gained in the United Kingdom or in the Overseas Dominions. There are many oases in Which research might be better undertaken by the parent society, or the committee in Great Britain, even though they particularly .affected the Overseas Dominions. Other matters of research which were initiated or desired by the home society might be better carried out in Australia, in Canada, in India, in

some oither overseas dominion, and so the foundation would be laid for a generalization of the scope of this arrangement, and for concurrent action such as I have stated.
Since that time, Australia has appointed a committee and an advisory council, -largely on the same lines, one has -been established and in .South Africa, and New Zealand is discussing and arranging for the appointment of an Advisory Council and a collaborating 'body. About a year ago the Canadian Government passed an order .by which a subcommittee was appointed in Canada consisting of the Ministers of Agriculture of Labour, of Mines, of the Interior, of Trade and Commerce, and of Inland Revenue. These were appointed because each with the exception of the Department of Labour, has more or less work of that kind going on now. The Mines Department, for instance, has one of the best equipped laboratories on this continent, although not the largest by any means. The Department of the Interior has, in connection with McGill University, a laboratory at work chiefly upon woods, their tensile strength', and everything connected with them. The Committee of the Privy Council was appointed to take in and co-relate all the Government branches or departments which have some such agency at work at the present time. The Department of Labour was added as well, because labour forms a very important part in this matter, and the -Minister of Labour was made a representative on that committee. Shortly after that subcommittee, following out the plan of Great Britain, appointed an Advisory Council of eleven members, consisting of three representatives of the industrial iamd business interests of the country, and eight scientists. Dr. Macallum of the University of Toronto, was appointed as the administrative chairman of this board. That Advisory Council was organized in December of last year, and has since been holding its meetings and going on with its work. I think it would be just as well for me to read an outline of the instructions sent by the Committee of the Privy Council to the Advisory Council. The memorandum reads:
This Advisory Council, in a memorandum from the Chairman of the Committee of the Privy Council, has been charged with the following duties:
(a)	To ascertain and tabulate the various agencies in Canada which are now carrying on scientific and industrial research in the universities and colleges, in the various laboratories of the Government, in business organizations and industries, in scientific associations or by private or associated investigators.

(b)	To note and schedule the lines of research or investigation that are being pursued by each such agency, their facilities and equipment therefor, the possibilities of extension and expansion, and particularly to ascertain the scientific man power available for research and the necessity of adding thereto.
(c)	To co-ordinate these agencies so as to prevent overlapping of effort, to induce cooperation and team work, and to bring up a community of interest, knowledge and mutual helpfulness between each other.
(d)	To make themselves acquainted with the problems of a technical and scientific nature that are met with by our productive and industrial interests, and to bring them into contact with the proper research agencies for solving these problems, and thus link up the resources of science with the labour and capital employed in production so as to bring about the best possible economic results.
(e)	To make a scientific study of our common unused resources, the waste and byproducts of our farms, forests, fisheries and industries, with a view to their utilization in new or subsidiary processes of manufacture and thus contributing to the wealth and employment of our people.
(f)	To study the ways and means by which the present small number of competent and trained research men can be added to from the students and graduates of science in our universities and colleges, and to bring about in the common interest a more complete cooperation between the industrial and productive interests of the country and the teaching centres and forces of science and research.
(g)	To inform and stimulate the public mind in regard to the importance and utility of applying the results of scientific and industrial research to the processes of production by means of addresses to business and industrial bodies, by the publication of bulletins and monographs, and such other methods as may seem advisable.
That sets out generally the plan and scope of the work of the Advisory Council, under the direction of the sub-committee, of the Privy Council. These eleven gentlemen are all honorary members. They are men distinguished in business or in scientific and industrial research and knowledge. They1 give their time entirely free; their travelling and working expenses are paid. It was felt advisable that it should, be the duty of one man to keep the machine in motion and to be the' general director of its energies, giving all his time and effort thereto. He has been denominated the Administrative Chairman, taking exactly the same position with regard to our Advisory Council as Sir William McCormick takes on the British Advisory Council. A salary of $10,000 is paid to Dr. Macallum for this work. In this way we get the services of eleven men of distinguished attainments and of great capacity who give -I can very well attest that they have done so during the last six months-a great deal of their valuable services to the working out

of the purpose set forth in these instructions. It is not the intention of the subcommittee of the Privy Council, of this arrangement, or of the Advisory Council, to duplicate work which is already going on. The intention is rather to prevent overlapping and to co-ordinate the work. The first work that they have undertaken is, in line with the instructions, to tabulate the scientific and research facilities, agencies and -equipment in Canadian educational institutions, and to communicate with and to tabulate in the same way those agencies and facilities, outside of the universities, which are possessed by private corporations, public bodies, or associations for scientific purposes. On the other hand, they are to find out from the industrial and productive workers of Canada what are the peculiar problems which meet them in their work, how far they are trying to solve those problems and what aid can be given them towards that solution. They are to distribute such of these problems as it is possible to the different industrial and research agencies which are already established and which are doing work in Canada. That has been carried on in a very effective way. I think it would be interesting to the House to have a very short digest of the methods they are pursuing to get that information. That information is very widely disseminated; it has to be sought in every part of . Canada, and it must be fully and accurately obtained if it is to be available as a reliable basis. Five or six great societies or associations have voluntarily banded themselves together for the purpose of getting this information: the Manufacturers' Association of Canada, the Canadian Mining Institute, the Chemical Society, and the Society of Civil Engineers of Canada, and an association of technical organizations of different kinds in Canada.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: Does this last technical organization already exist?

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext:
They are all in existence. The system they proceed upon is to prepare questionnaires which are sent out to all colleges and universities, scientific and research organizations, and are designed to secure in full the information to which I have referred. Questionnaires are sent'also to the managers of industrial and productive interests in Canada, the questions being so arranged as to bring out what these respective bodies are doing in the way of research, what are the problems which cause them difficulty, how far they are solving or trying to solve those problems, and how far aid may be required. This inquiry spreads itself over a vast number of organizations, industries and productive associations. These bodies, united for that purpose, appointed a central committee of sixteen. This central committee appointed a general committee of five to see to the distribution and collection of these questionnaires. They establish headquarters in the different provinces through the members of their organizations in those provinces. To make a long story short, the questions get into the hands of the parties for whom they are intended, but they are not left there without assurance that they will be intelligently and fully answered, to the largest maximum percentages. So that field aides and helpers voluntarily working from the members of those five associations are enlisting in the field some seven or eight hundred men whose duty it is to explain what' answers are required to the questionnaires - much valuable information can be given to facilitate the work of those who answer-to see that the questions are answered and that they are forwarded again to the central committee. These questionnaires have already been sent out, a large number of them are now coming in and the tabulation has been commenced. The House will see what a fund of wide, useful and accurate information will be in the hands of the Advisory Council when the questions come in and the information therein contained is placed at the service of the Advisory Council.
It is also of great moment that the man power which is eligible and available for research shall be multiplied in our Dominion. It is rather a sad thing that many young men who have come out from our different colleges and universities and who have developed strains of original research and scientific inquiry are later snapped up by concerns in other countries, particularly in the United States. Many of them are to-day doing yeoman service in the great industrial operations in the United States, some of them receiving princely salaries. On the other hand, we have had a very small number of such men, owing, I suppose, to our smaller development in rich industrial concerns and the lesser interest that has heretofore been taken therein. The result is that many of our young men have not been encouraged to remain and pursue their investigations and work in Canada.
One duty laid upon this Advisory Council is to endeavour to reinforce that staff in our own country, in the first place.



by creating an interest in industrial establishments. This interest is now rapidly being increased, the necessity for it being more and more seen and felt by our industrial operators. In this way there will be created a home, as it were, and a place for work and occupation in Canada. In the second place it is proposed to endeavour to reinforce that staff by taking hold of those young men before they have gone away, in so far as they have developed evidences of peculiar excellence in the way of research, and by a system of studentships and fellowships encouraging them for one or two years after they have come through their university or college, to take up and pursue lines of research. There are to be six hundred dollars studentships and twelve hundred dollars fellowships, and a limited number of those will be distributed, and the Advisory Council has for the last few months been trying to secure that class of young men in our different institutions who may be as it were pre-empted for that kind of work.	.
What I have said will indicate to the House what it is proposed to carry out under this system which has been inaugurated, which has its branches in all parts of the Overseas Dominions and which is being extended to India and to some of the protectorates as well. We have connection with the Advisory Council of Great Britain by assessors. One of the council is at present in Great Britain representing the Advisory Council as an assessor. He sits with the Advisory Council in. Great Britain while he is present there during the summer; he gets to know all that they are doing; he gets all the information and knowledge possible; in turn, he gives them information as to what we in this country are doing, and he keeps up the connection between the two bodies. Similar connections are being kept up with other Overseas Dominions. Sufficient has been stated to show that in this arrangement there is the beginning of a very strong, active and useful organization which, in the ways that I have mentioned, will enforce the lesson of the necessity for science, industry and production marching hand in hand. If that has been necessary in preceding years, it probably has never been more necessary than at the present time, and it will probably be all the more necessary after the war has ended and the adjustments of peace are brought about.1 Then, more than at any previous stage of the world's history, there will be the necessity for knowl-
edge and scientific help being given to the processes of industry and of production in order that the keen competition that is coming may be met, and that the utmost of productive output may be had. This is simply taking time by the forelock, bat none too 6oon, to get this system into working order in Canada and in this way to prepare ourselves as far as possible for the productive and industrial work of the future.
This organization was created by order in council, and this legislation is simply to put in statutory form the mode of organization which was adopted and passed by order in council.

The project
which has been elucidated by my right hon. friend is certainly well conceived, and the idea is a very commendable one. One feature which certainly merits my commenda-

speechtext: Is this Council to be .a permanent organization, or merely temporary?

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: It is not a temporary body at all. It is proposed to make it a permanent body amd to 'have the benefits of its services in increasing degree from year to year. The Advisory Council are following out closely the same plan that bias been adopted an Great Britain. There the Advisory 'Council get .into communication with the great engineering, scientific and metallurgical societies, steel plants and industries of that kind, and subsidiary committees, working 'together under the supervision of the Council, .are formed for the purpose of stimulating research and solving .the various problems that come up. Three standing committees bave .already been set up in Great Britain, the Metallurgical Committee, the Mining Committee, .and one other. Men eminent in these different lines have banded themselves together as committees 'and 'are working in co-operation with the Central Advisory Council.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: Although I am not opposed to the constitution of the Council at the present time-in fact, I think, perhaps, it is the best body that could be .appointed to do this work during tlhe period of the war-I .have no faith whatever in the ability of such .a body to perform the work of this nature that it is so desirable should be performed in this country. I do not think it is passible for a body of .scientific men meeting .at Ottawa only two or .three times .a year ito accomplish any results, .and I do not think any member of the Council thinks otherwise. I do not think any good results can be hoped for from similar .bodies in the United States 4 p.m. or in Great Britain, although I concede that practical results may possibly be expected in Great Britain, which is an older country. The distances there are shorter, and the men who are voluntarily giving their services can readily be brought together, and they may have a good deal of time to give to this sort of work. But in this country every member of the council is engaged in other work, and cannot do justice to ihis ordinary vocation and at the same time render any great service to the nation as a .member of the council. I am not however opposing the constitution of the council for the time being. I think the idea is a very good one indeed, but I hope the 'Government and the country will not commit themselves to the policy of making the council a permanent body. It can, however, blaze a trail for work to he done in the future by men who shall belong to the Cival Service of Canada, and who will be able to give their whole time to this research work.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext:
I am sure the House must appreciate very much indeed the splendid patriotic spirit that has actuated the members of the council in giving their services gratis for this work. I wonder, however, if any other motive played its part in the appointment of a council of an almost entirely honorary character. I fear that we in this country, and this Parliament espec-

ially, are actuated to a considerable extent by a desire not to spend money on such work as this. I quite agree with the hon. member for Halifax that at the present time it is perhaps all right to accept the *services of these men on the terms on which they have been offered, but I do not believe that any permanent useful organization can be built utp in that way. I hope the Minister of Trade .and Commerce1 and this. parliament will get aw-ay from .the old time parsimonious habit and be generous to this body. We should be ready to spend even hundreds of thousands of dollars on an organization that will do work that is not only necessary to this country at the present time, but which will bring vast profits to the nation generally in the future, if the work is carried on in an aggressive manner. I am sure that the personnel of the council is beyond criticism, but as the hon. member for Halifax has said, these men are all engaged in other work and cannot be expected to give u,p a large part of their time land energy to gratuitous work. I hope that before the next meeting of parliament the Minister o.f Trade and Commerce will lay a proper foundation for carrying out what must be regarded as a most extensive programme for .a body containing only two paid officials to carry out for the benefit of the nation. I trust that in the near future we sh.al.1 have in this country under ^ the control of the Government a vast institute for industrial and scientific rese.ar.oh. There is plenty of work for such an institute to do, work that would be of vast advantage not only to the manufacturing and industrial interests of the country but to the nation at large.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext:
Sufficient unto
the day are tire possibilities thereof. When I said "that this was a permanent organization I simply meant that it was not for this year only, for no man can tell what such an organization will grow into or what changes will be made. I think, however, all hon. gentlemen in this House will agree with me that an excellent beginning has been made. The first thing to do is to get a foundation of information and facts, and that is what these gentlemen have set themselves to do. They have agreed to pursue that until they do get this information and they have agreed to do it without pay as 'an honorary work for the country's benefit. What that may develop into one cannot tell.
.Mr. NESBITT:	What arrangement will
you make for transmitting * to the colleges and schools .any information they get?

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: The information they get is chiefly, at the first, for their own working out. It is not so much information for the schools or colleges that is contained in the answers to these questionnaires that have been sent out, which answers are now coming in and being tabulated. But results as they do accrue will be published in various forms so that the information may become available to all who are interested in it and in so far as it is a matter of public interest to the public as well. Neither is it to be thought that these eleven, or nine, men are going- to do all the research work themselves. I quite agree with my hon. friend that it is not possible for them to do that. They are chiefly the body which is to cordate and co-ordinate this information and form a plan which can afterwards be worked out. But, I think we were fortunate in getting gentlemen like- these to undertake the preliminary work. A great deal more of this work will have to be done in the future than has been done in the past if Canada is to hold her own.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: Who are the representatives of industry on this council?

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: Mr. Hobson of Hamilton, Mr. Surveyor, Mr. Bienvenue and Mr. Ross, who is a practical engineer. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Lanrier), spoke of the leaning which he rather had towards technical education; or he spoke of it as a matter that might be more generously and widely supported than it is at the present time. I think we .all .agree with him in that respect. But Germany itself has. shown instance where immense expenditures have been made on scientific and industrial researcn which to a certain extent prepares the way for the better working out of technical education in the; interest of the labourers, the artisans and the general working public. Numbers of these immense corporations in Germany have spent millions of marks themselves on scientific research, for solving problems the solution of which has given a tremendous impetus to all branches of industry in Germany. The same thing is taking place in the United States. Large industries in the United States are paying out millions and millions of dollars absolutely for this research and scientific work. We have done very little in that respect. We ought to do a great deal more but that does not preclude the substratum, the very important part, that my right hon. friend mentioned.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext:
I do not at all
condemn the idea which my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) advocates'-very far from it. In the United States and, indeed, in Canada, some of the large industrial corporations have special appropriations every year devoted to research and invention. I do not know how much they have spent in this way, but, especially in the United States, they have devoted very large amounts of money to these objects. In Canada large industrial corporations also have invention and research departments, but, I believe that the foundation of that work lies in technical education. That will afford the best basis for what you have now in mind.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: As far as I understand, the German Government assisted private corporations in their researches, but the private corporations were the ones that really carried on the research work and established industries which spread throughout the world. I know that this work has been carried on by private corporations in the United States. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce is quite right when he says that they have spent a large amount of money on their research department, but they are not going to tell you what they are doing. Is this council supposed to compile the information it gets from other people throughout the country? If a man has some secret in his business, he is not going to tell you what it is.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: We do not ask him to do that. These big German corporations spent large amounts of their own money upon this work.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: They did, but the Government assisted them.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: The Government assisted them, but much less than we have believed. We have a somewhat exaggerated idea of the amount of assistance that the German Government has given to industry, trade and commerce. It has favoured them by legislation rather than by expenditures. It has really been by expenditures, combinations and co-operation amongst producers themselves in Germany that they have brought about the great results that have flowed to German industry.

raw mia/terAal, wherever At may oome from, outside or inside of Germany, ox from foreign countries, it is manufactured and goes back to be sold ito the consumers, and in all this process there is ia close co-operation between the different corporations themselves, each feeding into and helping the other. subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: Would the minister explain what is meant by 'industrial research? speechtext:
No, At is just the other way. For example, when I was in Cobalt last summer, I saw employed a process for separating ores, which had lately been put in operation in the United States, and which had just gone into operation in Cobalt, called the flotation process, by which oil and water forming globules absorb, or rather encase, the fine metallic portions and float them. They are now working over the old dumps in Cobalt, which could not have been worked by any other process.
There was an industrial problem. There was this reservoir of value, to la limited extent, which was unutilized. What is the method by which that ore, An fine and distributed parts, may be recovered? Scientific investigation went to work upon that problem and ultimately solved it, so that now it is patent that a very greatly improved and qualitative process has been brought into this sphere of the world's production.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: That process had existed for many years, although it has been much improved in the last five years. subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext:
That is where
some of the most important advances are

to :be made in the work of development, in connection with what we may call those lame ducks. A process has been scented; it has been partly started, it has done a certain amount of good, but it has come to a point where nobody seems able to move it any further, and, while partly useful, it has not perfected its purpose. Then someone is needed to take hold of that and, by research and investigation, hit upon the thing that will make it a perfect rather than an imperfect process.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: I agree that that is where great help can be given, where an inventor arrives at a " fault " and cannot get any further. But how will this help that?

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: I explained the advantage that would be derived if we had, at the close of the war, as a result of the establishment of this council, twenty, thirty, fifty, sixty or one hundred agencies of research. My hon. friend will see that the method is one of finding out and co-ordinating, of compiling information and disseminating it, so that the best possible use may be made of all the agencies which exist in the country.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: Would it not be better to employ a staff of highly trained scientific men to carry on the investigations? That would not mean a very large expenditure. Our industries in this country are largely in a very crude condition, although, of course, there are some exceptional industries that are well organized and very effectively and scientifically carried on. We will require more science in our industry after the war than ever before, and I agree with my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Steele) that we should not be niggardly in starting off this important body. I am not sure that even to-day, when we must carefully guard every dollar of expenditure, it would not be wise for us to appropriate quite a substantial sum for the establishment of a corps of highly skilled scientific men.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext:
My hon. friend would find many difficulties. In the first place, he would find it absolutely impossible to get a dozen or twenty trained first class	scientific	men. You	cannot findthem	in this	country or any	other,at the present time. They cannot be got. I doubt if we could find half a dozen,	such as	we would like to	have.Then,	in order	to carry on	their	work,
these men require extensive and very elaborate equipment. We have in this 
country some of the finest equipments, although not the most extensive, and in these places you have trained investigators who, to a certain extent, will carry on these lines of investigation. We are trying, in the first place, to reinforce that small regiment of scientific investigators-I speak of it in that way because of their very small number in this country-and every man who can be got is being 'taken up by the industrial corporations.
I believe that this is the best possible way of initiating the matter and I think that in the future there will be very large and beneficent results. Some men in this country say we want a great central institute where you will have all of. these research operations carried on. That is very good, and that may come some time, but it would be tremendously expensive and difficult to man.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: We are not big enough for that yet. When the minister takes action he should get hold of some man. who has made a study of scientific organization and industry. That is one of the things where the United States have applied themselves for the last four or five years, with greater benefit towards the cheapening of the cost of goods than anything that has happened in many years.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext: No doubt about that.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH.
speechtext:
The minister has added another commission to the long list which this Government have appointed. Whenever there is anything to be thought out, instead of showing any initiative in grappling with problems by proper methods of organization, the Government have approached the matter by the creation of commissions. We are asked to stand round in admiring gaze and say to each other, "So and so, members of that commission, are working for nothing." That has been the case with several of these commissions. Somebody has been trusted with tremendous responsibility and willing to do the work for nothing, and the country is expected to believe some great work is to be achieved. What has become of the Economic Commission appointed last year, on which a large number of gentlemen were supposed to work for nothing except their expenses? Nobody has heard of anything they have done. Professor Macallum is a very worthy man indeed, and I have the highest personal regard for him. He would do good work, hut there is no use asking a lot of college professors from one part of Canada

to another to make a trip to Ottawa at a time when their classes are in session and all their energies must he devoted to the task of teaching young men who pay the class 'fees, and expect to get the best results. You cannot expect anything of a practical nature from a combination of that kind. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman from Halifax and the hon. gentleman from North Oxford when they point out that there is only one way to deal with this matter, and that is on business lines alone. These dilettante organizations will produce no results. We will get tired of-one commission after another, appointed to report upon matters, when the reports never come, and the business men of the country reach that point where they say there is no use bothering about it. Why should we not appoint two or three well-known scientists and retain their services, to work all the time, and then you will get good results. You will get no results from Professor Maeallum and these worthy gentlemen who visit Ottawa and lunch together, and then go back home and attend to their ordinary duties. subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.

speechtext: On the .motion of Right Hon. Sir George Foster for Committee of Supply:

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair I desire to discuss a report of great public interest which was laid on the table of the House on the 13th of this month. I refer to the report made by Commissioner Mr. W. F. O'Connor, K.C., which has been the subject of more or less discussion in the public press since the day it was made public.
I desire to congratulate the Minister of Labour upon having accomplished something in the direction -upon which he set out when he passed the order in council authorizing inquiry into the cost of living in the month of November last. Several abortive attempts have been made during the past seven or eight months to deal with the cost of living, but the report of Mr. O'Connor is the first -substantial benefit that has been derived from the activities of the Department of Labour since the war began. It had been called to the attention of this Government many times that the cost of living was bearing more and more upon the people and that in view of the extraordinary conditions arising out of the war, it was in the highest degree desirable that this Government should take action similar to that -taken by sail other belligerent countries. As early iais the session of 1915 ia motion was made- in this House by the member for Brantford (Mr. Goekshutt), 'asking for the appointment of -a food controller, or the taking of some other steps to -prevent undue enhancement of the prices of the necessaries of life, No -actiom was taken. Every session since then the matter has been di-s-cus-sed, bu-t with the same result. In the month of May I had the privilege of moving the -adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing the extraordinary rise in the price of flour and other wheat products that was manifested an that d-ay's
[Sir Wilfrid Daurier.l
market reports. Tihe Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), speaking fo-r the Government, intimated that -as s-oon 'as the Government of the United States should take action -along -that line this Government would take similar -action. Fortunately for this country, it did not 'take the Government of the United States as long to -act after it had become a belligerent nation 'as it took the Government of Canada. Some three weeks after wiar was declared by the United States a food controller w-as appointed in that country and legislation was introduced into both Houses of Congress giving him -ample power to deal with this question.
-Sir GEORGE FOSTER: Does my hon. friend say that that legislation -is yet passed?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: No, -but a food controller has been very actively on the job in the United States for miany months.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Who?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Mr. Hoover.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
Mr. Hoover has performed no single official act since he came back to the United States by virtue of >any authority conferred upon hi-m by Act of Congress.
Mr. KYTE.: He has not h-ad legislative -authority to perform any official -act, but his activities 'are manifest just the same, and the results of those activities have , been reflected here in Canada.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: So are the activities of my hon. friend, but they are not official.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
If the Minister of Trade and Commerce had directed the activities of his department into the channel in which we are all interested, perhaps better results would have been achieved.
What are the findings of Mr. O'Connor, the commissioner, in respect of the 'supply of foodstuffs? He investigated the operations of the principal 'cold storage companies, abattoirs and export houses in Canada and the effect of the operation of these companies upon the prices of bacon, eggs, cheese, beef, butter, pork, mutton and lamb are disclosed in the interesting report to which I have referred. On pages 3 and 4 of his report, Mr. O'Connor says:
A few of the cold storage companies, however, have attained such dimensions and have so centralized the business in certain lines that as respects particular commodities particular companies are able to exercise a practical monopoly, especially of export business.

That is the very danger that members of the House of Commons anticipated immediately after the outbreak of war. War brings about unusual conditions. It brings about large aggregations; it brings about big business. The citizens of Canada have been congratulated many times upon the tremendous amount of money that has been expended in this country since 1914 in the manufacture of war munitions. The enormous profits which have been made in that branch of industry appear to have whetted the appetites of gentlemen engaged in the manufacture of supplies not necessarily applicable to war operations. Following the lead of the manufacturers of munitions who have been enjoying large profits, manufacturers of and dealers in foodstuffs have been able to tuck away snugly equally large profits and dividends. Discussing the question of bacon, Mr. O'Connor has given some startling figures. The total quantity of bacon handled by twelve of the largest cold storage houses in Canada during 1916 was no less than 150,000,000 pounds. Of that total amount, 140,259,202 pounds were handled, exported, and sold by two cold storage companies.
The names of these cold storage companies were not disclosed in the report of the commissioner, but since its publication two companies that profess to have been injuriously affected or unfairly represented in that report have come forward and disclosed their names. These are two of the largest dealers in food products in Canada, and, inasmuch as they have disclosed their names so far as the report of this commission is concerned, I shall have no hesitation in taking the House into my confidence and stating that the two companies are Matthews-Blackwell, Limited, and the William Davies Company, Limited, both, I understand, having headquarters in Toronto. Out of the total quantity of 151,000,000 pounds of bacon handled, sold and exported in Canada during 1916, no less than 140,259,202 pounds were handled by these two companies, or 93 per cent of the total. Of this quantity the William Davies Company handled about 64 per cent and Matthews-Blackwell, Limited, about 29 per cent. On the subject of bacon, Commissioner O'Connor says:
With regard to bacon we And one company selling 97 millions of the total 1916 cold storage sales of 151 million pounds at a margin of 5.05 cents per pound. The margin of the same company the previous year was 3.67 cents on 57J million pounds. There is no evidence of correspondingly increased storage or other costs. Ninety-four million pounds at least of the sales of 1916 were for export. The margin
of 3.67 was sufficient, satisfactory and profitable in 1915. Why not in 1916? Company No. V it' will be observed sold 42J million pounds of bacon. Its margin was 3.56 cents per pound. The margin of its competitors was small. They were, however, feeding the home market. Its need was not so great. This bacon situation is in a class by itself and will stand some explaining.
We have heard it stated from time to time in justification of the creation of companies with large capital that by the operation of those large companies there would be a reduction of overhead charges and in the cost of operation, and that, therefore, the goods supplied by those large corporations would necessarily and properly be sold to the consuming public at a lower price. That has been the argument advanced every time the merging of companies engaged in the manufacture of foodstuffs or of other necessaries consumed by the people of this country was sought. But taking into account the immensely larger sales by the William Davies Company, Limited, and Matthews-Blackwell, Limited, in Canada in 1916 over preceding years, we are amazed to find that they were not content with the margin of profit earned in the years 1913, 1914 and 1915, but in 1916, when they did the largest business known in their history, they charged the highest prices that were ever paid by the consumers of this country.
At page 34, we have this statement from Commissioner O'Connor, referring to companies V and IX, which are the two companies I have mentioned:
It will be observed that the sales of bacon of companies Y and IX together cover 140,000,000 of the 151,000,000 pounds of bacon which were sold by all the cold storage companies of Canada during 1916. The total exports from all Canada according to the computations of the Trade and Commerce Department were for the same year 169,000,000 pounds. Possibly no more striking example of a monopoly of any one commodity can be cited from the trade records of any country supplying the Allies with food. These two companies are here mentioned together, but a distinction between their operations has already been clearly drawn with regard to their margins and the proportion of the quantity sold which was controlled by the respective companies. The cause which led to this unprecedented situation is not far to seek. The basis of a monopoly in this commodity existed before the war and the extraordinary conditions since have enabled its progressive development.
I turn to Table IV in this report, and I find that the margin of profit charged by twelve cold storage companies is given in one of the columns. Company No. 1 sold at a margin of 1.26; company No. 3 at a margin of 3.4; company No. 5-Matthews-Blackwell, Limited-at a margin of

3.65; company No. 7 at a margin of 1.6; company No. 9-the William Davies Company-at a margin of 5.05, and company No. 11 at a margin of 1.37. As I pointed out a moment ago, instead of large business and enormous turnover resulting in reducing the margin of profit and the cost to the consumer, we have here quite the reverse. The smaller cold storage companies that dealt in bacon during 1916 were content with a margin of profit varying from 1.26 to 3.65, but the largest dealer in bacon of all was not content with this margin of profit, but capped the climax by exacting a margin of 5.05 cents per pound.
The quantity of bacon sold by company No. 9, that is by the William Davies Company, was in 1913 approximately 85,000 pounds at a margin of 3.63 cents per pound; in 1914, 14,000,000 pounds at a margin of 3.6 cents per pound; in 1915, nearly
60,000,000 pounds at a margin of 3.67 cents per pound, and in 1916, nearly 100,000,000 pounds, at a margin of 5.05 cents per pound. The operations of company No. 5,-the Matthews-Blackwell, Limited-for the various years are as follows: In 1913, approximately 4,000,000 pounds of bacon were sold at a margin of 2.02 cents per pound. In 1914, more than 9,000,000 pounds were sold at a margin of 1.3 cents per pound. In 1915, nearly 30,000,000 pounds was sold at a margin of 1.2 cents per pound, and in 1916 more than 40,000,000 pounds at a margin of 3.5 cents per pound. The Matthews-Blackwell Limited following the lead given by the William Davies company increased its margin of profit from 1913 to 1916, notwithstanding that its turnover and the business transacted by that company in 1916 was far in excess of that of any other year of its history. The general margin for all the other cold storage companies of Canada has decreased from 1.06 cents per pound in 1913 to .7 cents per pound in 1916. With the exception of the two companies that I have mentioned, all the other cold storage companies doing business in Canada found their margin of profit was reduced. This illustrates the effect of active competition. The very reverse process has been exemplified in regard to bacon and the resulting higher margins. These are the two most striking examples shown in the records of the effect of competition in the one case and of practical monopoly in the other.
There are 110 cold storage warehouses in Canada operated by 67 companies. Forty per cent of the quantity of meat sold by the

three largest companies is sold to the consumers through their retail stores. One company has 80 retail stores; another company has 40 retail stores. These large cold storage companies are in active competition with the smaller tradesmen and the butchers in the respective cities in which their branch establishments are located.
One would imagine that the advantage would he altogether in favour of the consumer in respect of the prices charged by these large companies, because they have greater facilities for handling their products; they can turn out their product at very much less cost, and can derive a larger profit from the by-products in respect of the goods which they handle. They have an advantage over the small butcher in respect of distribution facilities and the manufacture of by-products. The proceeds from these by-products alone should have enabled the abattoir companies to sell at a very much lower margin of profit than the small butcher. But that has not been the case. The larger the business, the larger the price charged the consumer, and the larger the profit; that is the experience the people of Canada have gone through, the very bitter experience, I am bound to say, during the last two or three years.
Take the matter of eggs. The William Davies Company sold 5,566,505 dozen eggs at a margin of 7.27 cents a dozen during 1916, whereas the other cold storage companies investigated were content with margins ranging from 1.74 to 5.38 per dozen. The total trade in eggs was centralized in a few of the largest cold storage companies. We have heard a great deal of complaint throughout the country, and particularly in the larger cities, as to the price of eggs during the last year. The investigation made by Mr. O'Connor has disclosed the fact that the greatest offender in respect of boosting the price of eggs is the large cold storage company, and not the retail dealer. Previous to 1916 the margin of profit on eggs charged by William Davies & Company and other companies under investigation was very much lower than the margin charged in 1916. Commissioner O'Connor finds:
The disproportionate increase received by the cold storage companies as respects eggs and bacon would be Justified if storage costs had correspondingly increased, but the figures submitted by the various companies for the last four years do not evidence a sufficient rise in storage costs to bridge this gap, so the cause must be looked for elsewhere and found. The rise in the price of bacon in 1916 was clearly a result of a practical monopoly brought

about by a huge and unprecedented export trade demand.
As regards cheese, two companies alone sold over 50,000,000 pounds out of the 72,000,000 pounds sold hy all cold storage companies in Canada in 1916. The total sales of cheese by three companies 5 p.m. cover 70,500,000 pounds out of a total of 72,500,000 pounds sold by all cold storage companies in Canada during last year.
With respect to beef we have a similar condition of affairs. Of 170,000,000 pounds of beef that passed through cold storage last year, 124,000,000 pounds was controlled by the seven largest abattoirs; 99,500,000 was sold by three companies alone; 113,000,000 pounds was sold bj* four companies, and
60,000,000 was sold by American companies in Canada, for home consumption at a smaller margin, than that of the Canadian companies. That, Sir, is another striking feature of the food supply of this country. Dealers in beef on the American side of the line are able to supply the Canadian consumer with beef at a lower price than the cold storage companies of Canada charged in the year 1916. Before I am through with my observations I shall be able to show that the Canadian dealer in other food products is selling more cheaply in England to-day than to the consumers in Canada, because in Canada he has the advantage of a tariff which enables him. to boost the prices, whereas in England the products are sold in an open and free market.
With regard to fresh and salt pork, the commissioner finds:
The concentration of this meat in the hands of a few companies is almost as striking as in the cases of the other commodities mentioned, the margin of the seven abattoirs for fresh pork being larger than the common average. The same holds true of the totals for fresh and smoked pork , the margin of the large abattoirs being 1.94 cents per pound, the common margin for cold storage being 1.85; this in spite of the fact that the large abattoir has a very real advantage over the smaller, because of the former's superiors facilities for developing by-products.
There is another instance that the smaller company sold more cheaply to the consumers in Canada in 1916 than did the larger companies. On page 5 of his report Mr. O'Connor says:
I do not mean to be understood as stating that there have not been cases of undue profit taking. Quite the contrary, as will appear at a later stage of this report when I shall express an opinion concerning certain seemingly excessive charging, which in my judgment, is none the less open to criticism because, for
the most part, the commodities affected were destined for export to Great Britain and the
allies overseas	A very small profit,
per pound or per dozen, will produce quite an aggregate, all the same, when the operations of a company cover many millions of pounds or of dozens. For this reason it seems to me that such companies may well be content in such times as these with a very minute profit, per pound or per dozen, indeed.
That is a very severe indictment of the majority of these companies in respect of their dealings with the consumers not only of Canada but of the allied nations. We are all exerting our very best efforts in order that the Allies may win as speedy a victory as possible. We have heard it preached that during war time there should be no profits, or at all events, that profits should be reduced to a minimum. I think everybody in Canada will subscribe to that doctrine, but unfortunately those whom we would expect to be actuated by at least an equal degree of patriotism as regards a speedy and favourable determination of the war are not the first to put those doctrines into practice. Commissioner O'Connor finds that:
Individual instances of profiteering occurred during the year 1916. If they had occurred in the present year since the provisions of the Order in Council under which I am making this investigation, I would consider it my duty to recommend that the facts be laid before the proper Attorney-General for his consideration.
There have been instances of profiteering which were of a criminal character, the commissioner says, having regard to the order in council passed by the Minister of Labour some months ago, and it is only because that order in council was not in force during the period covered by his investigation that criminal proceedings cannot be taken against these companies. The commissioner states on page 32:
We have been paying more for most of our food for domestic consumption than the Allies to whom it is exported. This was not the result of patriotism, but something quite different	The proces in the home market exceeded those in the export market in 1916, for butter, by 1.82 cents per pound; for cheese, by 2.14 cents per pounds; for beef, by 1.24 cents per pound; for ham, by 6.11 cents per pound. For eggs, pork, and bacon thfe prices for home consumption were less than for export; eggs, by 3.76 cents per dozen; pork, by 1.08 cents per pound; and bacon, by 0.48 cents per pound.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
I am not going to enter into competition with the Minister of Trade and Commerce as regards playing the game fair. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) gave an illustration of how fair the minister played the game with him in connection with the investigation of the New Brunswick Central railway.
As I stated a moment ago,. the William Davies company have , given a statement to the public. They hurriedly rushed to the public press a day or two after the report of Mr. O'Connor was published, and, quite indifferent to the fact that Mr. O'Connor is a public official in whom the public repose considerable trust and confidence, they have this to say of the author of that report:
The author of this inquiry shows a strange lack of even a fundamental knowledge of simple book-keeping, and a dangerous inability to co-ordinate figures. The following are specific and outstanding errors in the report.
And they then proceed to discuss what were apparently errors. But there was no error because, as I have said, Mr. O'Connor made it perfectly clear that he did not wish to convey the impression that the 5.05 cents per pound was profit, but that it was margin only. And why was he obliged to resort to the statement? Questionnaires, as the Minister of Labour pointed out, were forwarded to all these companies at the time that Mr. 0:Connor undertook to make these inquiries. Certain information was demanded of each company, upon which information the commissioner would subsequently make his report. The Minister of Labour, speaking of this report, after having referred to the questions sent out, said at page 3798 of Hansard:
One or two firms said :	We cannot answer
these questions; we are not in a position to give you the particulars.

These were the particulars as to cost of transportation, insurance, cold storage charges from the time the commodities entered into the cold storage warehouse until they reached the point of consumption in Great Britain. The minister continued:
Hon. gentlemen will see that in the case of bacon that is sold in Liverpool the delivery charges would be a very important matter. No answer was given to that question by the firm about which there has been so much talk during the last few days.
The firm of William Davies and Company refused to give the information to Commissioner O'Connor, because as they said, they did not have the information, and yet they castigate and criticise Mr. O'Connor because he set down the marginal profit instead of the actual profit itself.
On page 63 of his report, Commissioner O'Connor says of the action of a certain company:
Its action was not In my judgment illegal, but was it respectable? Likewise as to the more aggravated, because continuous, exao-tion of excessive profits by another firm, on bacon; aside from the matter of illegality, is this sort of thing to he considered respectable? Mine may be as the voice of one crying in the wilderness, hut I have to register in the negative.	.
If it has been as the voice of one crying in the wilderness, it reached the ears of certain ministers of this Government who decided to appoint another inquiry to investigate the work of Commissioner O'Connor. What has Mr. O'Connor found in his report? He finds that as regards at least one or two of these companies there has been profiteering, monopoly, undue enhancement of prices to the consumer, and withholding of food for purposes of speculation. As regards the latter charge, a newspaper report says:
The increased holding of butter, eggs and pork are justifiable on the basis of an equivalent increase of sales since 1916, but that the increase of holdings of beef, bacon, ham, mutton and lamb are not justifiable upon that basis, and are speculative. Accordingly, he says the prices of these commodities should forthwith drop. The stocks of cheese, he thinks, are running too low.
Certain commodities then, according to this statement, have been kept in larger quantities than usual in these cold storage warehouses for the purpose of speculation as to how much further charges can he exacted from the consumer in respect of these commodities.
We have, as I stated, another commission of inquiry that has been constituted for the purpose, I thought, of doing the work that Mr. O'Connor said in this report he

had not time to do. But that is not the case. The statement made by Chairman Henderson in Toronto this morning is that they are going to conduct an independent inquiry quite separate and apart from the work of Commissioner O'Connor. Mr. O'Connor realized and appreciated the difficulties he had in estimating the exact amount of profits earned by the William Davies .company. He .said:
No specific data is given upon the point of storage costs, because it is believed that a special investigation is required into the value of the by-products of meat, and that some compulsorily applicable cost accounting system of storage and other costs on specific commodities should be established.
He says the means. for providing such an expert examination is under way. From that I judge Mr. O'Connor was continuing his investigation for the purpose of ascertaining what was the exact margin of profit earned by the storage companies under investigation, and no one is better able to complete the inquiry than Mr. O'Connor himself. He has been in charge of this work for six months past. He conducted an enormous volume of correspondence. Fro-m his report I gather he was in correspondence with, over a hundred cold storage companies, export dealers and abattoir companies in Canada. His work was not completed, inasmuch as I have said the actual margin of profit was not determined by him, but I cannot understand this Government, instead of supplying Mr. O'Connor with the accountants to enable him to get the proper information which was required, and which was called for under the circumstances, discarded Mr. O'Connor's services altogether, and called Mr. G. F. Henderson,
K.C. I am bound to say that the selection of Mr. Henderson has not been a very happy one for the Government. His appointment was up for consideration a few days ago in this House, and while I have nothing to say as to the standing of Mr. Henderson at the bar of this province, or as to his ability and capacity to discharge any obligation that might properly be imposed upon him by this or any other Government. A few months ago Mr. O'Connor held an inquiry in the city of Ottawa as to the cost of certain food products, and the solicitor who appeared foT the company upon trial was G. F. Henderson, K.C. He was retained several months ago by companies that were the subject of investigation by Mr. O'Connor, and I repeat, to say the least of it, the selection by the Govern, ment of Mr. Henderson as the chairman of that committee to revise the work done
by Mir. O'Connor is a most unfortunate one, and I fear it will not have the confidence of that portion of the people of this country who are most interested in the results. I pointed out the other evening that Mr. Henderson appeared a year ago in the city of Ottawa as solicitor for interests that are, to a certain extent, allied with the interests which are on trial at the present time. He appeared for Colonel Allison before the Royal Commission appointed to inquire into certain contracts for the manufacture of fuses which Allison obtained for his confederates, from the then Shell Committee. The Shell Committee was disbanded, and the Munitions Board was appointed, and, to say the least of it, I think the Government should have guarded themselves against appointing Mr. Henderson, the solicitor for Colonel Allison, to act as chairman of the committee of the court of appeal, in which Sir Joseph Flavelle, the chairman of the Munitions Board, is more particularly interested than any other person, as against the interests of the consuming public of this country. The Government instead of taking immediate action to mend the matters complained of, as affecting injuriously the consuming public, both in Canada and the allied countries, appoint this new commission for the purpose of inquiring into a matter which is entirely subsidiary and quite apart from the main finding in Mr. O'Connor's report. Mr. O'Connor found there was monopoly, undue profiteering, improper withholding from the public certain foodstuffs, and that the food business in respect of certain lines in this country, had got into the hands of companies that were exacting larger prices than other companies of a similar character dealing in the same quality of goods. The question as to the actual profits made by the William Davies Company on the bacon sold by them is not the most important question. The important question is that there is a monopoly, that there is profiteering, that there is undue enhancement of prices, and while the consumers of this country are still suffering under the disabilities and disadvantages arising from those conditions, this new commission of which Mr. Henderson is the chairman, is leisurely whiling its time away in the city of Toronto, and nothing is being done to relieve the situation as it presents itself to the consumer at this moment. The commission met to-day in the city of Toronto, pursuant to notice. I have a report of the transactions as published in

the Ottawa Journal to-day. It reads as follows:
Mr. Walter L. Breckells has been appointed secretary of the Commission.
The Commission consists of of Mr. Henderson, as I stated, and Mr. Brodie, and Mr. Clarkson, two accountants. The report proceeds:
No evidence was taken this morning and an 'adjournment was made, probably for two weeks, "pending reports on the examination of the packer's books.
There has been an ladjournmamt of two weeks, and inasmuch >as it took Mr. O'Connor .six 'months to get the information which enabled him to present the report which he h,as forwarded to the Government, what guarantee have we that the present Commission will complete the work in a shorter time? We will have a whole year gone by land nothing done, no .action taken to relieve the situation which Mr. O'Connor discloses. The Teport proceeds:
Mr. Louis Heyd, barrister, who said he represented the consumers, asked if Mr. Clarkson "was a member of the firm of Clarkson, Gordon and Dilworth, paid auditors of the books of the Wm. Davies Company.
Mr. Clarkson replied in the negative. Mr. Heyd said that he knew that Mr. Bain had the ability to conduct the investigation if he only had the inclination. Mr. Bain promptly replied that he had the inclination and a little more.
Mr. Heyd announced his immediate retirement when the chairman stated that Mr. Clarkson's old firm in which was the latter's father, had audited the company's books ten years ago. He said he had no desire to take further part in the investigation if there was any connection between a member of the commission and the William Davies Co.
I submit that under those circumstiances this is another incident which shows that another of the selections made by the Government an the matter of this Commission is mot the most fortunate one that could have been made. It may be argued that although the Clarkson Company 'audited the books of the Davies Company some ten years ago, that a representative of that company ought not to be prevented from acting on that Board. But I say that if there is an .accountant to be had who never had anything to do with the employment of the William Davies company, the Govern,menit should have sought him out and avoided this suspicion, which will go- abroad when the circumstances surrounding this appointment are made known. Mr. Tilley, who acted for the Davies Company, said he wanted an opportunity to criticise Mr. O'Connor's report .and the -means by which he arrived at his conclusion. Fancy ! They wanted to criticise the means by which Mr. [Mr. KyteO
O'-Connor arrived a)t his conclusion. The consuming people -of this country are not concerned as to the means by which he arrived at this -conclusion. Is it true that there is monopoly, profiteering, undue, prices charged to them and -that cold storage products are being kept in the warehouses for the purposes of speculation? These are the matters in which the -consumers of Canada are concerned, and upon that subject there is no controversy, and no denial. The report proceeds:
We would not have been here to-day, said Mr. Henderson, "if there had been more frankhess." He, however, pointed out that they were not investigating Mr. O'Connor, but were making an inquiry independent of the report."
So that whatever credit the Minister of Labour is entitled to for having appointed Mr. O'Oonn-OT to make a report upon the food -prices in Canada, that credit is immediately taken -aw-ay from him by the appointment, by his colleagues in the Government, of Mr. Henderson and two accountants who are going to proceed to have another inquiry, altogether. What -are Mr. Henderson and -his -accountants going to inquire -into, in which the public have any concern? They are not so much concerned in w-hait was the actual amount of -profits which this company obtained on the sale of products. That can as well be dealt with later as now. The o-rder in council does not disclose any other purpose for which the Commission was appointed. I have a copy of the order in council appointing this latter board of inquiry. It reads, in part:
The minister represents that returns have been made to him under such regulations by the William Davies Company, Limited, and Matthews-Blackwell, Limited, the first-named company being No. IX mentioned at page 30 of said sessional paper, and the second-named company being No. V also mentioned at said page 30, and that the said companies have taken exception to the said report so far as it concerns them.
It is because these two companies have taken exception to the report that this new commission has been appointed; the public who are concerned in the disclosures which Mr. O'Connor has made are not to be considered in the maltter at all. The order in council proceeds:
The minister considers that the circumstances disclosed by such returns and in said report which recommends further investigation of the dealings of the aforesaid companies justify such investigation and examination of the premises, books, papers and records of the said companies as is in and by said regulation No. 6 provided.

Then they proceed, under the terms of the ordler in council passed last November, to provide that the Commissioners shall investigate as follows:
(a) The amount of margin between the first cost to each of said dealers and the price ultimately realized on sale or disposal by each of said dealers; (b) the net profit; (c) the specific elements or factors which have conduced towards or which have operated to produce the difference found between such margin and such net profit, indicating the extent of the operation of each element or factor; also to recommend in writing to the Minister of Labour a standardized system of costs accounting applicable to the business of cold storage, from the operation of which system the net profits of cold storage companies within Canada may from time to time be readily ascertained.
Not a word of authority is issued to this commission by this order in council to inquire into or to verify Mr. O'Connor's assertion that there is monopoly, that there is profiteering, that there is undue profit, that there is undue withholding of food products from the public for purposes of speculation. All these considerations are thrown to the winds; the report which was prepared so laboriously and so completely by Commissioner O'Connor is thrown into the discard until another report shall (have been made by a more favourable court, upon which the Government may or may not take action, according as the spirit may move them when the proper time comes.
This is not the first time, Mr. Speaker, that the people have been handed out a gold brick in respect to legislation, taxes, and conditions which bear unfairly upon the consuming public. Take for instance, the excess profits tax. A great deal of credit was claimed by the Finance Minister a couple of years ago when he imposed his business profits war tax. It was pointed out by members on this side that that tax would, in the final analysis, be paid not by the company, but by the consumer. We know that the dividends of these companies increased enormously in the years 1915 and 1916 after the business profits war tax had been levied. The companies, by reason of the increased prices which they have exacted from the Canadian consumers, are able to pay the business profits war tax without suffering any loss. As a matter of fact, their dividends, after they deduct the business profits war tax from their earnings, are greater now than they were before that tax was imposed. The same thing is true with regard to the imposition of the increased tariff of 71 per cent in the session of 1915. It was pointed out that while a
limited amount of revenue would be obtained from the imposition of this increased tariff, what the Government would receive would not be at all comparable with the increased profits which the manufacturers would exact from the consumers of Canada by reason of their ability to add 7ipc. to their prices. In that respect the consumer, no person else, pays the tax. The tax upon patent medicine, banks, the .taxes levied upon railway corporations-ail these have come down to the consumer. If a person goes into a drag store to-day to buy a bottle of proprietary medicine, in addition to the price which he otherwise would pay, he has to pay two cents war tax. So that the poor man who buys the proprietary medicine is the one who pays the war tax, not the merchant or .any other person who handles that medicine from the point of manufacture to the point of retail distribution.
*I will refer to page 35 of Mr. O'Conhor's report. He says:
The quantity of bacon sold by company No. IX was approximately, in 1913, 85,000 pounds at a margin of 3.63 cents per pound; in 1914, 14,000,000 pounds at a margin of 3.6 cents per pound; in 1915 nearly 60,000,000 pounds at a margin of 3.67 cents per pound, and in 1916 nearly 100,000,000 pounds, at a margin of 5.05 cents per pound.
So .that as the war taxes were increasing, the margin and the profits were increasing in the treasury of the 'William Davies company. That illustrates what I pointed out a few moments ago: that the operations of the war tax levied by the Finance Minister have the effect of increasing the cost of the commodity to the consumer and the result to the company is that they earn larger dividends than ever before.
Another matter in which that part of the country from which I ooime is interested is the matter of salt. I called the attention of the Finance Minister a week or so ago to the great necessity that existed in the fishing communities of Nova Scotia for an adequate supply of ;salt. .The Minister Of Trade and Commerce then made ia statement to the House which went to show that the Government was unable to do anything. But the Government of Newfoundland was able to do something. From day to day the Government of Newfoundland are causing ships laden with salt to arrive in the fishing ports of Newfoundland, and the result is that the fishermen are able to cure their catch-a catch which has been larger and' more profitable to the fisherman than at any time in the colony's history.
