subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: The fact is that the Government of Newfoundland took the matter in hand, and their fishermen have salt; the Government of Canada took the matter in hand, and the fishermen of Nova Scotia have no salt.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: The Government of Newfoundland took the matter in hand, but the British Admiralty proffered ships for this purpose and set the price of freight; no doubt the people paid that price, and got their salt. The Government of Canada took the matter up with the Admiralty. The Admiralty agreed to have the ships put at their disposal and placed a price upon the salt as to freight. As I understand it, the Canadian fishermen could not see their way clear to pay that freight; consequently they did not get their salt.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
The result is as I said: the Newfoundland Government got salt for their fishermen, but this Government failed to get salt for the' Canadian fishermen. When I -called the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the matter in the House, he ended his remarks by saying. that the Government did not have -a peck of salt. The obvious rejoinder to this facetious remark on the part of the minister would be to say that the lack of salt probably accounts for the advanced condition of decay in which the Government finds itself. If it had more salt, it would be better preserved.
SiT GEORGE FOSTER: My hon. friend would require all the salt that is in the ocean to keep him sweet.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
If the necessity on my part for salt is in proportion to the ' freshness of the Government, I shall require a great deal.
There is another matter in which the j c.ople of this country are taking a more 01 less languid interest. Leading members of the Government have been in favour of a coalition, that is to say, a coalition Government with the "coal" out of it, by which I mean the fire, glow, power and masterful energy of my right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I said the leading members of the Government are in favour of a coalition, because it is well known that the stars of lesser magnitude, whose light would

be extinguished by an equal number of Liberal members who would be brought in to take their places, are not wildly in favour of coalition. But, while the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are beating the bush to find Liberals who can be led or driven into the Government, they are preparing the way for a "Win-the-War" Government which shall comprise both political parties, by filling the vacancies in another branch of this Parliament out of Conservatives of the deepest dye, principally recruited from the ranks of the supporters of the Government in this House. The people of this country are beginning to wonder whether or not all this question of coalition is really honestly meant and seriously intended. It appears to me at this time when, at all events, some people in this country have an open mind on this question-and I had an open mind on it until it was absolutely closed by the conduct of the Government in appointing their partisan supporters to all the vacancies in the Senate a few day? ago-if they wished actually to bring about a coalition of both political parties in order to form a Government to win the war, at least they would have shown their good faith by going "fifty-fifty" upon the appointments of senators instead of corralling all the appointments as they have done.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: We had to get a "fifty-fifty" first.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
What is the Government going to do about the O'Connor report? They have appointed another commission, Mr. Henderson, Mr. Clarkson and Mr. Brodie. These gentlemen are not authorized to deal with the matters in which the people are most seriously concerned. They are not authorized to deal with the indictment which has been presented by Commissioner O'Connor against the cold storage companies of Canada. It is of no consequence to say, except as an incident, what the actual profit of the William Davies Company has been. That can be dealt with in another way and at another time. The interest and concern at the present time of the people of this country is how they are going to get rid of this monopoly; how they are going to get the necessaries of life at least at as low a rate as the Allies are paying for them, after shipping them 3,000 miles across the ocean. 'They want to know when this profiteering is going to cease. The O'Connor report as regards these matters stands as it was delivered in this House on the 13th of July, and the people of this country will demand instant action from

the Government in order to remove the disabilities and the hardships from which, as ' Mr. O'Connor has informed this House and the country, the consumers of Canada are suffering at the present time.

Therefore, it is scarcely fair or proper to discuss this matter at this time, as it is really sub judice.

Another commission
will be right on the heels of this one. When are we going to discuss the question?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend referred to that the other day, and I pointed out to him the provisions of clause 6 of the order in council. He knows better than to speak about another commission; he knows .that clause 6 of the order in council provides for this further investigation, and the order in council, .as read iby my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) provided for ait, so that it is in vain to speak about more commissions inquiring into what the present further investigation may find.
I am very much surprised to see my hon. friend from Richmond, who is a lawyer, finding fault with the appointment of Mr. Henderson as one of these examiners. The only objection my hon. friend gives is that Mr. Henderson, last winter, when a similar investigation was being held by Mr. O'Connor in Ottawa, acted for one of the merchants interested. If that came from a man who never saw a lawyer or knew nothing about them, I should not be surprised, but my hon. friend knows as every lawyer knows, that the best lawyers of the country are on one side of a case to-day and the next day are taking up the other side of a similar transaction. He will find one of the "best lawyers in Toronto defending a notorious thief to-day and to-morrow he will find him prosecuting a notorious thief. For a lawyer to fiud fault with the appointment of Mr. Henderson as a member of this commission because he appeared before Mr. O'Connor last winter to see to it that a merchant of this city had an opportunity of getting all his evidence before
him, is to say the least of it, most extraordinary. My hon. friend's argument will have no weight with the intelligent people, lawyers and others, of this country.
My hon. friend said on more than one occasion that Mr. O'Connor had found that there was hoarding and excessive accumulation on the part of those cold storage companies for the purpose of holding cold storage commodities until they should rise in price. If he will look at page 62 of the report from which he has been reading, he will find these words:
I And that the operations of cold storage companies generally have been fairly conducted. There has been no illegal combination nor any excessive accumulation on the part of any company.
Notwithstanding the fact that my hon. friend had that statement before him, he repeated several times in this House this afternoon that Mr. O'Connor found that there was hoarding and excessive accumulation with a view to getting an enhanced price in the future. I need only refer to that to show how unreliable and untrustworthy many of the statements made by my hon. friend this afternoon really are,
His statements in many respects were not a fair representation of what Mr. O'Connor says in his report. He says that Mr. O'Connor found that there was a combination. Th,e truth is that Mr. O'Connor on the very first page says that " there is nothing like combination among the various companies. There is a very lively competition, instead." He found that theie was no combination, no hoarding and no excessive accumulation.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: If it is .such an excellent report, why did the packers find fault with it.

speechtext:
I am not speaking for the Davies Company. Again on page 5 Mr. O'Connor .said:
On the whole the operation of the cold storage companies have stood the test of investigation well. The profits per pound or per dozen of most of these companies have been small, and have not to any degree contributed to produce the very high prices prevailing.
The mistake my hon. friend from Richmond made, and it has been made by many, was in confusing margin and profits. This afternoon my hon. friend used the two words indiscriminately. Mr. O'Connor is very particular in his report to point out that he is not dealing with profits at all, but with margins.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Is there any difference made in the report between gross profits and margins?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
In works on economies, and by expert accountants the word " margin " means the difference between the ooist price of an article and its selling price. In this particular case it would include the cost of cold storage, cost of delivery, overhead charges, etc. In the case of bacon delivered in Liverpool, for instance, the cost of delivery would be a very large item, especially at the present time when tonnage is so scarce. Mr. O'Connor points out in his report:
It is desirable that the precise meaning attached to the word "margin" in this report should be very carefully noted. It represents gross, not net, profit on the commodity from the time it is laid down, all costs and expenses paid, in the storage warehouse. The questionnaires sent out to the various companies to secure specific information on margins demanded sworn testimony as to (a) the quantity of each commodity purchased during the year; (b) the cost of such laid down in warehouses, including freight and unloading charges; and (c) the total quantity sold during the year and the total amount for which sold. The average cost prices and average selling prices were computed. The difference between these is the margin referred to. The margin represents, therefore, the cost of storing, losses, interest on investment, overhead charges, any other expenses incurred by the cold storage company from the time the commodity enters the warehouse until it reaches the persons to whom they sell and the cold storage company's profit. It is the total charge imposed on the food from the time it enters the cold storage house until it passes into the hands of grocers or wholesale dealers.
He therefore made it perfectly clear that he was not dealing with net profits at all.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock, I was pointing out that Mr. O'Connor distinctly stated that he found no evidence of a combine in all his investigation of the 110 cold storage plants in Canada; that he found no evidence of hoarding or excessive accumulation, and that the management of the various cold storage plants in Canada had not materially contributed to the enhanced prices of cold storage commodities. He, himself, had in this Teport recommended that an expert accountant should be employed to make a further investigation to get the details of what he calls " margins."

He pointed out distinctly in his report that he was unable to ascertain what the net profits were until he had particulars of the margin, the margin including, in the case, of a cold storage plant, overhead charges; cost Oif delivery and cost of .selling the goods. In the case of bacon, about which there has been so much said, the margin includes the coat of delivery in Liverpool, a very important item. In reading Mr. O'Oomnor's report, you must bear in mind that he is not speaking of net profits; that it will be necessary to ascertain the particulars of these margins in order to find what the net profits were; and that he reeomr mends the appointment of 'an expert accountant for the purpose of ascertaining the details which he did not have to enable him to come to a fair conclusion.

I am not prepared to say why but they did not give it. Mr. O'Connor recommended in his report that an expert accountant be appointed to ascertain what the net profits really were. We have appointed for that purpose Mr. Brodie, the leading member of the firm of Price, Waterhouse and Company, and Mr. Clarkson, the senior member of the firm of Clarkson, Dilworth and Company, accountants of Toronto. They are both firms of national reputation. I have no doubt they will make a thorough investigation and give a report which will command the confidence of the whole people. I am not here for the purpose of defending the William Davies Company but I am here for the purpose of seeing in so far as possible that the report made by Mr. O'Connor is not misrepresented. I am anxious that the whole of the evidence should go in. I had in my mind, when .the order in council was passed last November, the idea that if we got these statements under oath for the four years and from month to month afterwards it would be a great check on business and would go a long distance to prevent any undue enhancing of prices. I have great confidence in publicity. I believe the work of the department has done a great deal in that direction already. This report will do a great deal to keep profits down to where they ought to be. We are continuing to get reports every month and we expect to continue on that line.
The hon. member for Richmond pointed out that according to Mr. O'Connor, with the smaller dealers, the margin did not rise as rapidly as it did with the William Davies Company for instance. That is very easily explained. The small dealers were not exporting their stuff to Liverpool. Any one who knows anything about the condition of trade knows that ocean freight rates have gone up by leaps and bounds during the last year or two.
It costs eight, times as much to transport sugar from Cuba to Montreal as it did before the war. I do not know what the proportion is for the carrying of bacon across the Atlantic, but it is reasonable to suppose that the ocean freight has risen very rapidly, and that would tend to widen the spread or margin between cost and delivery price in Liverpool.
It was said that some statements which I made on the 4th June were in conflict with Mr. O'Connor's report. Nothing can be further from the fact than such a statement. I was then combatting an argument made by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) that because this company- as was stated in a telegram which the hon.

member had received, which was subsequently denied by the president of the company-had endeavoured to insure $2,000,000 worth of commodities in their cold storage warehouse, therefore there was excessive storage and hoarding. I did not deal with margins, profits or prices. Mr. O'Connor, in the last words of his report, said that he found no evidence of a combine or of hoarding or of excessive .accumulation. Thus there was no conflict between my statements and Mr. O'Connorjs findings.

They 'hoped that he would say: I cannot make out a full report as far as these people are concerned; I have not the necessary data. But Mr. O'Connor is a keen lawyer. He did the very best he could. He took parallel cases, and, using the evidence that he gathered in these parallel cases, he made a final report as to what the profits were. Then the howl came; then came the rush, like that of the Gadarene swine, to the Government. They said; "We have nothing to do with this man; away with him; crucify him ! Give us an absolutely new court; this objection which may be clearly urged against ns will not apply to a new court. We have no right to come into Mr. O'Connor's court; we have barred ourselves from it; there is no law of evidence or practice by which we can come in. Give us a new court, and we will come in with the new evidence." But even if the company had thrown up their hands and said: We do possess the information; we are willing to give you the evidence to complete Mr. O'Connor's report-what should have been done? No specific data is given upon the point of storage costs, because it is believed that a special investigation is required into the value of the by-products of meat, and that some compulsorily applicable cost accounting system of storage and other costs on specific commodities should be established. That does not mean that a new court is necessary under a- new order in council, and a new investigation beginning at the very foundation of things. He simply says that an inquiry should be made into one single phase of the question and that the project of providing such expert examination is under way; that is, an examiner is being appointed by his own department. When that portion of evidence was furnished, the whole thing was complete; that was an end of it. I cannot agree with the course now taken by the Government. They are throwing away entirely the six months' labour of this faithful servant of the Labour Department. They are discrediting his report, saying that it cannot be accepted ais arriving ait 1a true conclusion'. Accordingly, a new court is established, which will start all over again. The minister objected strongly this afternoon to my even suggesting that the matter would be kept indeterminately in the air by the^ holding of one investigation on top of another. I rnusit confess that that is what iit looks like. If the person who is affected by an investigation howls somewhat loudly when the report comes in, a new commission is appointed and from six to nine months' respite is given to the offender, who can go about without even seeking one dollar of bail. .
I suppose the Minister of Labour did not know that a judicial inquiry had been promised in this matter. We discussed this subject on the night of July 20, and the next morning a dispatch was published over the signature of the Prime Minister promising a judicial investigation.

The William Davies company gave to the minister, through his commissioner, this information, which is found on page 30 of this report, but they did not give him the information which would have enabled the country to have obtained all of this information without the second commission. They refused to give him the information which the minister says the Matthews-Bliackwell and other people furnished. If the Davies company had given .this information in answer to question B we would have had all the facts, and Air. O'Connor could have given us, beyond the shadow of a doubt, exactly the amount which the William Davies company made, because he has given to us the amount which M'atthews-BLackwell made, as he had the information relating to their , case. Matthews-Blaickwell's statement is given .as No. 5 on page 30. Their margin was 3.65, whereas by the application of the same figures that were applied in Matthewis-Blackwell case, Where you add the cost of storage and the cost of delivery, which the Davies Company did not give, we find that the William Davies company made 5.05 cents profit, or nearly 2 cents ia pound more than than Matthews-Black wel 1 did'on their sales. Mr. O'Connor goes on to tell us wb^at the margin is.
The just character of a margin on any commodity is dependent upon (1) the expenses incurred in 'storing, handling and selling such commodity, (2) the demand for the commodity for export and for home consumption, and (3) the general condition of the market, so far as it affects replacement values. Storage handling and selling costs have risen somewhat but they are comparatively a fixed non-fluctuating charge.
Mr. O'Connor was able to make that statement because Matthews-Blackwell and several others of the storage people had given 'him the figures. He goes on to>
say:
No specific data is given upon the point of storage costs, because it is believed that a special investigation is required into the value of the by-products of meat, and that some compulsorily applicable cost accounting system of storage and other costs on specific commodities should he established.
What is the. significance of that statement? It is that Mr. O'Connor tells us

that, applying the Matthews-Blackwell figures, the William Davies company Charged over li cents or nearly 2 cents a pound more for the same thing than Matthews-Blackwell charge, and which are included in their figures, 3.65. We have further this fact, that what Mr. O'Connor recommended was not a commission such as this Government has appointed, but a cost accountant who could go to the William Davies company and, by reason of his experience in cost accounting, get the exact figures which they had refused to give, although Mr. O'Connor had received them from these other people. What is the difference between an auditing accountant and a cost accountant? Every one having experience in business knows that an auditing accountant is one who examines the books kept by the accountant or secretary of a company to see whether the proper charges are made, whether the accounting is done properly and whether the profit and loss account has been correctly worked out He never gets behind what is on the books. But the function of a cost accountant is to go into every detail connected with the cost of production. That is entirely apart from the question whether the William Davies company's books were properly carried on by their clerks. The man who is paying 52 cents for bacon, is not interested in that problem, but he is interested in what their pork cost them and what price he is called on to pay for it in the finished state. Mr. O'Connor has given us what they paid for it, and what they got for it. He has received information, according to the minister-who has promised to give it us tomorrow-of what Matthews-Blackwell had to pay for cost of storing and for the. intermediate handling, which would enter into the difference between the price they paid and the price they received.
'The William Davies company had it but they did not give it. Why did not the minister, under the plenary powers which, if he did net possess them, could have been conferred upon him under the War Measures Act, before Mr. O'Connor's report was given to the pujblic, exercise those rights, and why did not he demand from Davies, and compel him to furnish the information which Matthews-Blackwell and the other men furnished? But the minister did not do that. He employs a dost accountant to get the information they would not give, but which the other people did give. Mr. O'Connor says:
Likewise as to the more aggravated, because continuous, exaction of excessive profits by an-

other firm, on bacon; aside from the matter of legality, is this sort of thing to be considered respectable?
My hon. friend the Minister of Labour, without going to the trouble of sending for the cost accountant to get the information which, he ought to- have got, gives this country the report of Mr. O'Connor. He seems to be excusing Mr. O'Connor, and yet he puts his imprimatur on Mr. O'Connor's report. Either Mr. O'Connor has told us what is true, or he has told us what is not true. If he has told us what is not true, he should be dismissed; and if he has told what is true, then the minister has been derelict in his duty because he did not apply the cost accountant and get the missing data which Davies did not give him, and which Matthews-Blackwell and the others gave. If he had got that information the country would have known whether there was profiteering or abnormal profits in the storage of bacon or not. But the minister gives this report to the public, which the public are bound to accept as correct, and which, I am sure, the minister does not question, even now. I asked the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) the other day in regard to this matter, whether in dealing with this proposition and the appointment of this commission, he intended to reflect in any way upon Mr. O'Connor. The minister (Mr. Cro-thers) shakes his head; and agrees with that position. If that is so, where do we stand? We stand in this position; that bacon from the retail stores of this country costs 52 cents a pound; that Mr. O'Connor has reported, replying to the intermediate question, the data which he had from Matthews-Blackwell, as to the cost; and he tells us that this concern is making 5.05 a pound upon every pound of bacon which they sold.

I want to discuss this question as something which is very much bigger than the William Davies company. It goes a great deal further, and calls for attention on very much more important ground. 'This country is face to face with a very serious condition in the matter of the cost of living. From the monthly reports issued by the Labour Department, it is clear that the cost of living in Canada has increased at least fifty per cent within the past five years. Some little time ago I made a calculation and offered it to the i-iouse, to the effect that the burden of the cost of food upon the people of Canada had increased by an amount of approximately $250,000,000 a year, as compared with five or six years ago. This is a burden on industry that can only be carried by increasing the values, or the price, of the product of industry; it is putting Canada absolutely out of the race as a country of industrial production.

speechtext: The cost has gone up in the rest of the world, just the same.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: I say most emphatically that it has not; that Canada is to-day an example of a country more thoroughly and completely under the control of monopoly, trust and combine than any other country in the world, and more under that control in the matter of its food products than it is in regard to any other product.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: That is not the question at all. The question is whether the rise has been as rapid in other countries since the beginning of the war as it has been in Canada. In the great majority of cases-especially in the belligerent countries, but also in some, neutral countries- the rise elsewhere has been more rapid than it has been in Canada.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
That would be no excuse for the condition in Canada, even if it

were the fact. Let us admit for the sake of argument, that it is the fact. Canada is an export producer; these countries' are import consumers. In normal times, there is absolutely no parallel between the conditions in Canada, a country which is an export producer of food, and tho'se in a country which is an import consumer of food.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: What about the United States?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
Everybody knows that
the cost of living is less in the United States than it is in Canada.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
Yet my hon. friend
wanted our products to go' in there free because they would get a better price.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Precisely, because Canada, as I say, is in the hands of the little ring of combines and monopolies, centering in Toronto and Montreal, who stand between the producer and the consumer. As a matter of fact, the producer in Canada gets less and the consumer in Canada pays more in all staple lines than is the case with the producer and the consumer on the other side of the line. About that there is no argument.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Surely the hon. gentleman is aware that the difference between what the producer gets and what the consumer pays is greater in the United States than it is ot ever has beem in Canada?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
There is no use in my discussing the matter with my >hon. friend, because my information is absolutely to the contrary. My hon. friend cam verify the facts by visiting the United States at any point along the bionndiairy line. He will find that the staple necessaries of life are cheaper in the United States than they are in 'Canada, and he will find that the producer receives a better price than the producer in Canada.
Mr. WRIGH^J: I miay inform the hon. gentleman that I have studied the question, both 'in the United States and in Canada, to ias great an extent as he has.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
Then there is no use in our discussing the matter any further. I am compelled to maintain the position that I have stated; it is absolutely in accordance with my knowledge of the 'facts.
The minister has seen fit, land very properly, to make lan investigation of the cost of food, particularly those classes of food
which pass through the cold storage establishments. Such 'a large proportion of the food of the people does pass 'through these establishments tHat necessarily the question .of the haindling of the food and the profits made during the process of its (passing from the producer to the consumer is an important consideration in settling -the question of the high cost of living. The minister as to be commended for having appointed a commissioner ias the first step in the effort of the Government, .assuming it to be making that effort to reduce or secure .a reduction in the cost of living and to put 'the Canadian consumer in the' position iin which he ought to be, but in which he is not, because of the existence of this combine amongst those who handle the production, preparation and distribution of food.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: In his report Mr. 0 Connor finds that there is no evidence whatever of a combine amongst the 110 cold storage plants in Canada.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: I do not wish to discuss Mr. O'Connor or his merits or his report; I am commending the minister for having appointed an investigator. I shall not discuss the question whether Mr. O'Connor is an efficient investigator. But it is a fact that Canada, a country of export production, has paid more for the necessaries of life under normal conditions than a consumer of the same necessaries of life three thousand miles away on the other side of the ocean.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Was that not true long before the war?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
Yes. I do not know what the condition is at present. I would hope that what I have said is not true of the present, but I am afraid that it is. The member for Richmond has given figures to the House to show that it is true to-day; that notwithstanding the abnormal cost of transport across the ocean, we pay as much in Canada to-day for the products that we export as the consumer in Great Britain does. That is a condition for which there is no justification. It is not a condition which arises out of the law of supply and demand. Mr. O'Connor may find that th^re is no combine amongst the food handlers in Canada. I do not care what he finds in that regard. If it is a fact that the home consumer in Canada pays as much as the foreign consumer after the cost of transportation has been added, that is a condition that should not exist; it is not



in accordance with the law of supply and demand, and it should be made the subject of Government regulation and control in some way. It is not for me to dictate or suggest how that control should be exercised.	.
But it is not a fair proposition that the Canadian consumer of a Canadian product which is produced for export should have to pay. not the same price, but a higher price than the consumer art the other end of the market across the ocean has to pay. Such a condition of things is plain highway robbery. It could not take place unless there was a combine, no matter what Mr. O'Connor sayis, and it is the business of the Government and of the Minister of Labour to ensure that that condition shall not continue to exist.
I commend the minister for his appointment of Mr. O'Connor, but I protest to the minister against the delay of further investigations. Mr. O'Connor was an official of the minister's department. He took long enough, in. all conscience, to make his investigation. He has made his report. His report in some particulars is not very definite. He sets out a certain condition of facts which absolutely hears out what I have said in this House to-night. It is np to the Government and to the minister to take, action in this matter to-day-not to-morrow, or next month, or six months hence-and to tell the House and tihe country wbart action they purpose taking.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: It is admitted by every one that a very important part of the expenses has not been given. The oust of cold storage, the cost of delivering the goods in Liverpool, the marine insurance and the cost of selling have not been given. Would my hon. friend have us take action before we get those particulars and know exactly what the net profits aTe? Those accountants have been appointed to get all those particulars so that we may have complete information.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
If Mr. O'Connor is entitled to all the bouquets that he has been handed, having been six months on the job, he should have had complete information for the minister.
Mr. CROTHER'S:	He has recommended
?hat an expert accountant be appointed.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
I am not concerned with Mt. O'Connor; I tam concerned with the minister and with the Government. Here is a report which makes a certain statement of facts in regard to a certain matter. I imagine there is no necessity for a further

investigation in regard to some of those facts.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
The report does not
pretend to be complete.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
It ought to be complete.
I hold the minister and the Government responsible for its not being complete enough to enable the Government to take action. After the report of the commission which was composed of an employee of the Government appointed by the minister, the other commission appointed is, to my mind, not a commission for the purpose- of carrying out an investigation; it is a commission along the same lines as the Sir Charles Davidson Commission.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is
familiar with the order in council passed last November and iwith clause 6, which says, in substance, that when a return is made to me, I may appoint an examiner and authorize him to examine the books of the party and take evidence from witnesses under oath and so on. If he reads the order in council appointing these accountants, he will see that it is recited in that order that this is being done pursuant to the order in council of November last, so that this is simply carrying out the instructions we have under that order in council.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Why did not the minister make the companies give the information in the first place?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
We might have sent
an expert accountant at that time.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
I do not wish to enter
into a criticism of the details.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: I would like my hon. friend to go into the details.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
The statement made by
the minister is subject to the interpretation that when the first order in council was drawn it was drawn with a view to enabling a further postponement of action to take place. That is the onfy possible conclusion to place upon it.
To summarize what I have said, we are dealing with the biggest question that Canada has to face to-day. We have before the House a report, the result of six months' work under the direction of the minister himself, and, instead of our getting action under that report, all we get is another commission of inquiry. That is not what this country needs at the present time, and it is not what this country de-

mands. It is not in line with the action that the same Government takes in regard to other matters. For instance, let us take the action of the Government in regard to the control of the distribution of wheat. We have appointed a Board of Grain Supervisors to control the wheat trade of Canada. They can take possession of all the wheat in all the elevators of all Canada at any time. They can sell it to whom they please, when they please, at what price they please, and they can do more than that; they can prevent the export of grain from Canada. Is that the result of an investigation by a special commissioner such as Mr. O'Connor in regard to the cold storage business? I do not know whether it is or not, but I know that this authority has been placed in the hands of the Board of Grain Supervisors and that they have taken action under that authority. There is as much money involved in the action that they take as there could be involved in dealing with those cold storage estblishments. On the 27th of July the Board of Grain Supervisors fixed a maximum price at which the wheat of the crop of 1916 could be sold after the 1st of August. Why is it not just as competent for a commissioner appointed by the Minister of Labour or by the Government to fix a price at which Sir Joseph Flavelle shall sell his bacon after the 1st of August? What is the difference? There has been much more investigation in the case of Sir Joseph Flavelle than there has been in the case of the wheat, but in the latter case the Government have taken action and in the former they have handed us a commission which simply means that they are not going to take action. Let us have action in both cases. At the moment, I am not complaining about the action in the case of the wheat, but if we are to have the greatest industry of all Canada placed under mandatory control, such as the wheat trade is placed under, then there is no reason why this other article of food should not be placed under equally mandatory control. The Board of Grain Supervisors have gone further than to fix a maximum price for wheat after the 1st of August. It seems that the price of wheat is higher in the United States than it is in Canada. My hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Wright) will, I hope, not challenge that statement.
I find from the Ottawa Citizen of this morning that on July 28 No. 1 Northern cash wheat was womth $2.39 in Winnipeg, which is 1 cent below the maximum price
250J
as it will be after the 1st of August. In Minneapolis cash wheat was $2.90, and in Duluth $2.93. There was a difference of 50 cents a bushel between Winnipeg and Minneapolis and Duluth on Saturday lost. Now, remember that the maximum price in Canada only was to take effect after the 1st of August, .but the fixing of that maximum price depressed the price in Canada to 1 cent below the maximum figure, namely, to $2.39 instead of $2.40. Naturally, the owners of wheat in Canada would want to ship to the United States and get the benefit of that 50 cents a bushel. Now you can ship at least 1,000,000 bushels a day, and at 50 cents a bushel that would mean half a million dollars a day that the wheat traders could have made by shipping wheat from Canada to the United States.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: What would it cost to ship the wheat from Winnipeg to Minneapolis?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: I could not tell my hon. friend, but it is just the same rate-

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: It would not be 50 cents a bushel.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: What does my hon. friend understand by No. 1 Northern Minneapolis?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: I understand wheat of No. 1 grade.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Is it our Canadian Northern?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: It 'is an American Northern.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: That As a different thing. Kansas wheat is coming in just now. That is the reason.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: I think that would be a reason the other way. If Kansas wheat is coming in now if would depress the price at Minneapolis, but at Minneapolis the price was 50 cents 'higher than at Winnipeg for an inferior class of wheat, because their No. 1 Northern is not equal to ours.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
There is probably an error in the quotation from Minneapolis.
Mr. OnlVER: There is no error, beoause the quotation is about 'the same for Minneapolis and Duluth.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
There never was a
spread of 50 cents before.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Why do not our farmers simply send their wheat down there?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
That is exactly what I was coming to. The reason, is that this same Board of Supervisors have put
10 p.m. on a prohibition against shipping wheat to the United States.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: That prohibition is not in effect yet.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: It is in effect.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Not until the first of August.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: It is in effect now. It was put into effect before the 1st of August to prevent this wheat going to the United States and taking that 50 cents premium in price.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: That would be for the benefit of the working man in Canada, who would be getting food cheaper.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Not necessarily so. Unfortunately, the miller has the same call on the wheat that Sir Joseph Flavelle has on the hogs, and as between the price of the wheat that goes into the mill and the price of flour that reaches the consumer that is where the 25 per cent dividends of the Ogilvie Milling Company comes in. The farmer does not get the price for the wheat that the consumer pays for the flour, any more than the farmer gets the price for the hog that the consumer pays for the bacon.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Flour is free.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Yes, it is.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
Admitting that flour is free, bran and shorts are not free, anyhow. As a matter of fact the Government has taken authority, and has exercised that authority, in regard to the most important product that Canada has, absolutely to control the price, and not only the price but the sale also. It is not simply that they have taken the power, but they have exercised that power, and it is costing the holders of wheat in the West at the rate of half a million dollars a day from the time it was put into effect up to the 1st of August. I am not arguing at the moment whether that was wise or unwise, right or wrong. Although I hold that it was wrong as wrong could be, yet, for the purpose of my present argument, all I say is that the Government that could put its hand on the product of a western farm, first to fix a maximum price and next to prevent its export, when it was not prepared to handle the wheat or to protect the Canadian consumer in the milling of that wheat, has no 	! i | |J
warrant for saying that it cannot regulate the price of bacon just as it cduld regulate the price of wheat.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman be in favour of the Government fixing an arbitrary price of $1.50 a bushel for Canadian wheat instead of $2.40? That would be for the benefit of the working man.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: I am not discussing that at the moment.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: Would you advocate that?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
I shall have to allow my hon. friend to make his own speech, and ask him to allow me to make mine. What I want to say is that the Government cannot shelter itself behind all kinds of commissions from dealing with this question of the high cost of living, as it is affected by the abattoirs and the cold storage establishments, when the Government had taken means to control the price of that other great food product, the wheat of the western farmer. What they can do in the one case they can do in the other, and if they were wrong to do it in the one case, they should not do it in the other.
My hon. friend asked me about the cost of wheat and flour to the eastern consumer. Does he suppose that the eastern consumer gets that flour at the price the farmer gets for his wheat, any more than the eastern consujmer gets his bacon at the price the farmer gets for his hogs? No, he knows that standing between the produce^ and the consumer is the miller in the case of wheat, and the pork packer in the case of bacon. Does he not know that the price the farmer gets for his wheat or hogs has no relation to the price the consumer pays for his flour or bacon?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
My idea is that in view of the high cost of living the Government has been far ton generous in fixing the maximum price for wheat at $2.40 a bushel. I think if the price had been fixed at $2 or $1.75 or $1.60, it would have been a very veTy advantageous price for any farmer to get for wheat for which he had only been getting $1 or $1.10 a bushel. If any one should complain, it is not the farmer in the West, but the working man. In my opinion the price is altogether in favour of the farmer.
Mr. OLIVER; That is not the point I was discussing.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: That was the point I was discussing.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: It is quite competent for my hon. friend to say what the western farmer should get for his product.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: The high cost of living does not matter?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: The point I make is that no matter what the farmer gets it is not what the consumer pays, and that the eastern consumer pays without regard to what the western farmer obtains.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: You say so.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
It is the fact. Where do these pork-packing establishments and these milling companies get their dividends if they do not get them out of the producer on the one hand or the consumer on the other? What this Government should do is not to prevent, the producer from getting a fair price for his product, but they should prevent the middleman, the miller, the pork packer and the cold-storage man, from stealing from the producer on the one hand and from the consumer on1 the other. That is the duty of the Government, and the Government would be well advised to take that position. I must say to my hon. friend that, in my humble judgment, he is very unfortunate in making the suggestion as to a limitation with regard to the price that the producer of the West should receive for his wheat. In this particular season, it is to be regretted, but I am afraid it is likely to be true, the western farmer will receive a very small return on the amount of his crop. If he gets $2 or $2.50 for his wheat, it will not give him a return such as he could get a few years ago at a much less price. That is unfortunately the condition, and why should not the western farmer, with that unfortunate condition looming up this year, get the price that the markets of the world will afford him? You ask the western farmer to increase his production, but the only way you can get him to increase it is to give him a profit on the production he has. It is a shortsighted and most unfortunate policy on the part of the Government that they should exercise that power which is placed in their hands for the purpose of deliberately depressing the price of the farmer's. product below the price that the markets of the world properly afford. Such action cannot be justified under any circumstances, and particularly it cannot be justified under the circumstances of this present year. I am perfectly satisfied for the Government to have the control that it has under the War Measures Act. I am perfectly satisfied that it should exercise that control under certain circumstances. But I say that when it exercises that control under
the circumstances which, unfortunately for the country, exist this year, it is not justified and should not exercise it at the present time. But having exercised that control as they have, it is utterly and absolutely without excuse that fifty 'allow the pork barons to go on heaping up profits as they have done and taking them out of the producer 'and the consumer, one or the other. It is not only in the case of wheat that my hon. friends have seen fit to act. They fixed the price of newsprint paper. I iam sorry that my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. McOreia) is not here, because if he had been he rw,ould have enlightened the House on that pnatter. But the Government fixed the price of newsprint >and then they held an investigation. In the case of pork they neither fixed the price nor held an investigation that has any termination to it. There is only one answer to all that, and it is that the Government is part of that combine, which to-day is putting Canada out of business as an industrial country, is making the rich richer and the poor poorer, and notwithstanding the flood of war money is leaving the country worse off than it was before.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: What are the powers of the Food Controller? Has he the power to fix the prices of food commodities ?

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: I would not like to undertake to say offhand. His powers are very fully defined in the order in council appointing him. I think he has power under certain circumstances to fix prices, but I would not like to state it without having the order before me. It is a rather lengithy document.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
I would suggest that the minister acquaint himiself with the powers granted the Food Controller because the investigation of Mr. O'Oomnor will be for nothing unless there is somebody to enforce the recommendations of his report. Mr. O'Connior, on page 62, states that:
Now that a Pood Controller has been appointed and very close co-operation established between that official and this branch of this department, I consider myself relieved from the making of any suggestions as to the amelioration of conditions as I may find and disclose them, deeming that the function of action concerning food prices and food conditions, as distinguished from that of investigation, is now his to perform, and that any recommendations of mine, even though valueless, or because so, might prove embarrassing. He will be furnished with a copy of this report, and all data secured on the investigation'or to be secured will be (as he has requested, and

as you as minister have directed) will be at his disposal.
I assume .that when Mr. O'Gomnor made this repent he felt that he was not in a position to make recommendations for the amelioration of the conditions which he was investigating for the reason that immediately before making his report a food controller had been appointed who would have absolute authority to regulate prices. If the minister does not know whether the food controller has these powers, and if this report has not been transmitted to him, the work of the commissioner is absolutely valueless. I would like to 'ask the minister what he proposes doing in this regard? Surely he does not mean that his commissioner shall do work that is unproductive and useless to the nation? The report has been before Parliament for isome weeks, and surely that report has come into the hands of the food controller for action.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: I would like to remind the hon. gentleman (Mr. A. K. Maclean) that the minister (Mr. Crofhers) has exhausted his right to speak.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend, the Minister of Labour may speak with the consent of the House, and I am sure there will he no objection to his again having an opportunity to speak. I have one other word to say before the minister rises to make any reply. This report has made it abundantly clear that this second investigation is absolutely unnecessary and purposeless. Mr. O'Connor has made it very clear in his report that he did not attempt to find what were the net profits of 'those engaged in connection with the food products which he has had under investigation. He makes it much clearer than I thought he had-my information was largely from the newspaper summaries of the report that ihe was dealing merely with the margin between the buying and selling prices. He recommends that to ascertain what were the actual net profits an accountant be employed. That is a very fair recommendation, and with the assistance which in this particular' case the William Davies Company could render the accountant the whole matter could be closed up, I would imagine, in the course of a few days. Therefore, as the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) pointed out, a commission seems to be absolutely unnecessary and serves no good purpose; it means an expenditure of money by the country and delays action on the part of the

minister or the food controller. I think the minister should rescind the appointment of the commission by the Government. It is not too late for him to recall the appointment. All the information could have been secured by the appointment of one cost accountant. I submit that the minister has not justified the appointment of this commission. It seems to bave been appointed to suit the purposes of one of the manufacturing concerns whose .business operations were the subject of investigation by Mr. O'Connor. They seem to have demanded it and the Government seem to have acceded to their request, but I say that there was no reason or purpose in doing so.
Mr. CR0THER1S: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.
speechtext: By the unanimous consent of the House there can be no objection to the courtesy being extended to the minister of a reply; but if there is any objection it is not competent for him to speak again.

subtopic: REPORT OP W. P. O'CONNOR, K.C.- DISCUSSION BY MR. KYTE.

subtopic: WIDENING OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY.
WIDENING OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very much disappointed this afternoon at the answers of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) to the questions I asked him. I feel satisfied that the people of Prince Edward Island will also be much disappointed. The minister seems to lack knowledge in regard to transportation conditions between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, and in regard to the quantity of produce that should be moved from that province to the mainland, and the very short period of time, under present conditions, given to the people to move it. Previous to 1911 we were making some progress in the improvement of our transportation facilities. A company having a small subsidy of $12,000 a year had supplied two very efficient steamers to carry on the trade in the summer season, and the Government had provided two very capable ice-breaking steamers to do the work in the winter season. Shortly after the present Government came into power they undertook to change these conditions and to improve the system, which had not been giving entire satisfaction. They decided to establish the car-ferry system, that is to provide a steamer, to carry loaded cars between the island and the mainland. We were told that this could be finished in two years, and that then the Prince Edward Island Railway would be standardized to conform with the gauge of railways on the mainland so that cars could be loaded at the point of shipment and carried right through, loaded to the point
of destination. This would avoid the heavy charges and delay caused by the double transfer of freight between car and boat. This promise of standardizing the gauge was repeated by the Government year after year. Considerable delay was experienced in the building of the terminals, but we were looking forward to improvement when they should be completed. In this expectation the people of the island submitted without protest to the sale of the two winter steamers to the Russian Government. It was pointed out too that it was for war purposes, and we were willing to submit to a good deal if it was to the advantage ot the Allies in the great conflict. We were thus asked to make a greater sacrifice than any other province was asked to make, and we submitted without a murmur.
When the contract with the company to which 1 have referred terminated, the Government did not renew it, and they allowed one of the steamers, the better one, owned by the company, to be sold and to leave the service altogether. The Government bought the inferior one and kept her in the service. We are told by the Minister of Railways that the Government has no intention whatever of proceeding with the standardizing of the Prince Edward Island1 railway. He has not even stated that it would be undertaken at some time in the future, he held out no hope whatever. The car ferry will be of little or no use to the people of that province, until the gauge on the Island railway is widened, made to correspond with the gauge of the railways on the mainland. We will still have to transfer from car to oar, and again from ear to car, which will be no improvement over the former system, when we had to transfer from ca.r to steamer, and from steamer to car. The minister intimated that we might not even have the use of the steamers now plying between Summerside and Point du Chene, and the small steamer plying between Charlottetown and; Pictou, once1 the caT ferry comes into operation. If these steamers are taken off, and if we have to depend entirely on the car ferry under the conditions I have pointed out, transportation will be practically tied up altogether, and the people of Prince Edward Island will not be able to market their produce this fall. One of the great advantages of having the gauge of the Prince Edward Island railway widened would be that we could get refrigerator cars in which to load our perishable products, and therefore they would be comparatively safe during the month of Novem-
394(1

ber, thus extending the period of shipment. With the narrow 'gauge railway, we shall be obliged to ship to the terminal points in. the ordinary cars, subject to frost and rot, 'but chiefly subject to frost, and subject to all the conditions that may be occasioned in that way. Last season a very large quantity of potatoes were frozen in transit, just because of the conditions that I have pointed out, and these potatoes were a total loss, to the shipper in most cases. And it was an ordinary season. The railway protects itself, because it provides on the bill of lading that it will not be responsible for frost, and the shipper has to. take all the risks. The minister this afternoon stated that one of the objections to widening the gauge of the railway was that the bridges would have to be strengthened. Surely that objection could have been raised at any time during the last five or six years, just as well as it can be raised now. The minister must have known that the bridges would have to be strengthened when he gave the promise time and again that the gauge of the Prince Edward Island railway would be widened. If the steamer plying between Summerside and Point du Chene and the small steamer plying between Charlottetown and Pictou be taken out of the service, it will be simply impossible to handle the freight at any one particular point. Last year we had two steamers working at Charlottetown, the car ferry and the Stanley.
We had also the Northumberland at Summerside and yet the congestion of freight was so great, and these perishable products were kept waiting so long, that they were destroyed. They were in bad condition even before the frost arrived. They were weeks on the road. The steamers could not take them across to the mainland, and finally when they were taken over it was so late they were caught by the frost and lost completely. Last spring the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance advised the people in every way they could to increase production, that it was very important under the conditions in which we find ourselves to-day that the food production of the country should be increased by every possible means. The farmers of Prince Edward Island took that advice to heart, and this year the acreage under roots is much larger than it has been for many years. The crop looks well; the prospects are good, but what is the use of producing if you cannot get to market? Under these circumstances, the widening of the gauge of the Prince Edward Island rail-

way might be fairly classed as a war measure. Food is essentially necessary for the European countries now at war with Germany. Therefore production is most important in this country. The farmers of Prince Edward Island have done their share, but if the service is to be tied up and our produce is not to be carried across the Northumberland straits, what excuse can the Government give? I know the time is short. Not much can be done this year, but at least an effort can be made to do something, and the Government should give a definite promise that the steamers the Northumberland and Arranmore will 'be kept in the service between Prince Edward Island -and the mainland, and that all the assistance which the Government can give will be given to the people of that province to move their products this year. The Government, however, will not, 'and the Minister of Railways does not, give that promise; they hold out no 'hope whatever. The Minister of Railways seems to take the attitude, when you speak to him on .a business question in the ordinary affairs of parliamentary life, that you 'are offending him. He gives that impression. He has an irritable disposition land becomes 'apparently offended right off, and almost offensive in his remarks. Perhaps he does not feel that way, but it as unfortunate when we have business to transact with him in this House. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways have given the excuse that money is scarce in these serious times, and when we are at war we must economize, and that is given as a reason why the standardizing of the Prince Edward Island Railway has not been undertaken. But only a few days ago $3,000,000 was voted for some work on the Hudson Bay railway and for terminals at Port Nelson. That is not an urgent matter. I doubt very much if the terminals at Port Nelson will ever be any good. My firm conviction is that all the millions which have been spent and the millions which will be spent at Port Nelson will be thrown away. At any rate, that project can wait for a little while, but the matter to which I have drawn attention is very pressing >and cannot -wait, without inflicting great injury and great loss upon the people of the province from which I come, and to some extent loss upon all the other provinces as well. I think this question is of greater importance and 'advantage to the people of Canada as a whole than itihe question of purchasing the Quebec and Saguenay railway.

speechtext: I guess you aTe right about that.

speechtext:
I do not know that there is any particular work for the Government to do once they take possession of the Quebec and Saguenay railway. It is certainly not going to carry any produce from Quebec to the Labrador coast or to the more settled portions of Canada. If we are short of money, as no doubt we are, that is a railway that might very well wait while we proceed with things that are of far greater importance and far greater urgency, and, at the same time, carry out the promise of the Government. The Minister of Railways does not seem to be much exercised over the fact that the Government repeatedly made promises in regard to this matter. Now he deliberately throws the project to one side. The large expenditure that has already been made in the building of a car ferry steamer and of the expensive . terminals at Cape Tormentine and at Point Borden, will be of little use unless the whole work is completed. I make this statement to-night in the hope that it will reach other members of the Government, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) who, I think, would possibly take a little more interest in this matter than the Minister of Railways appears to take. This is one of the things that the members supporting the Government and the senators and all representatives from Prince Edward Island should take up with the Government; they should not allow it to go on in this way. The matter is so important to the whole of the people of that province that the Minister of Railways should not dismiss it in the cavalier manner in which he put it to one side this afternoon.
I see the senior member for Queen's county (Mr. A. A. McLean) in his seat. I know that he took a deep interest in this matter some years ago. I remember his stating at a meeting that the whole work would be completed within two years from the time that it, was commenced. The hon. member . may have honestly thought so at the time, but now five years have passed, and the work is not yet finished. The members from Prince Edward Island should not allow this matter to rest where it is at present. We shall have at least 3,000,000 bushels of potatoes to dispose of this fall, to say nothing of cereals and other products of various kinds. We have very valuable fisheries but we cannot develop them properly until
we are able to ship in cold storage, or in refrigerator cars; and this we cannot do until the gauge of the Prince Edward Island railway is widened. What has already been done is of no use whatever until the whole project is completed. The transportation facilities that we formerly had have been upset; communication is not as good now as it was some years ago, in consequence of the disarrangement that has taken place. It will remain that way until the gauge of the railway is made to correspond with the gauge of the line on the mainland, and until we can ship right through from the point of production to the point of destination. I shall be pleased to hear'from the sudor member for Queens county on this subject; perhaps he knows something about it which he would wish to state to the House.

subtopic: WIDENING OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I have listened with interest to the remarks of the member, for Kings county (Mr. J. J. Hughes) in this matter. I find that he disagrees with the member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). The member for Pictou a day or two ago expressed the view that it was not necessary to have the gauge of the Prince Edward Island railway widened; he thought that the matter should be left over until after the conclusion of the war. So that two hon. gentlemen who were supporting the Liberal Government for many years and who never did anything in the matter, differ on this subject. Now that the work has been initiated by the present Government, the member for Kings comes before this House and finds fault. I regret as much as any man that the war has come on and that this work has been stopped. I did all I could to induce the Minister of Railways and the Government to proceed with this work. I .am told, however, that the cost of the war is so great and the money stringency eo pressing that if is impossible to go on with these large public works. Since 1912, when 'the Government initiated this work, a terminal has been built at Cape Tormentine for this oar ferry. The Government purchased the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island railway, at great expense. They built on the Prince Edward Island 'side of the Straits of Northumberland a great public work to receive the traffic between Cape Tormentine and Prince Edward Island. They purchased a car-ferry steamer, the Prince Edward- Island, at an expense of between $800,000 and $900,-

000. This boat has done great service to Prince Edward Island; she has kept' up oommiunioartion better than any beat we ever had. It is true that the communication was between Pictou and Charlottetown. I do not east any reflection npon the port of Pictou, but I think that when the terminals are completed between Cape Traverse ;and Carletom Point and Cape Tor-menfcine, we shall have ia better service than has been had between Piotou and Prince Edward Island.
The hon. .member states that the work which has been done is of no practical value, owing to the fact that the gauge of the railway has not been standardized. I do not agree with him in that. I believe that the promise made by the present Government in 1912 that they would finish this great public work will be carried out. But we must take into consideration the present money stringency; we must take into consideration the fact that a war is on, and that every cent that Canada can obtain from all the various resources at her disposal is being used for war purposes. We must remember, also, that great public works have been stopped. The. works on the 'Welland canal and on various other undertakings throughout Canada have not been proceeded with actively. I understand that a very small sum of money is 'being used to keep up the work on the Hudson Bay line. The amount now being devoted to that work is infinitesimal compared with the total amount necessary to complete it. I have urged on the Government right along the necessity of at least partially completing this work by standardizing the road between .Charlottetown land Garleton Point and between Summer-side and Garleton Point. I think that that is all that is necessary at the present time. Different boards of trade in Prince Edward Island have made representations to the Government to standardize the gauge of this' portion of the road. I understand the amount to be expended in that work would be only about $250,000. If we can show the Government that the gauge of those portions of the road can be standardized for that comparatively small amount of money, the Government would probably go on with the work. Neither I nor my colleagues have been idle in making representations to the Government to undertake that work. I can, of course, see that if an election comes on, the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. J. J. Hughes) will have a great big flag to

wave; that he will say that the work which the Government has undertaken has fallen through, and that it will never be proceeded with. That will be his cry.
