While many orders for returns have been issued during the last three months in regard to this important department of Militia, the minister has not brought down any of those returns except the one that he brought down to-day relating to the expenditure on a site in British Columbia. It is usual, before Supply is obtained, that information of that kind should be given, and I am rather surprised and disappointed at not receiving it. While no one on this side of the House desires to obstruct the passage of the minister's estimates, the minister owes it to the House to bring down those returns. Time after time, there have been placed on the Order Paper questions that might easily be answered by the department through the minister, and the minister has said: " Stand as order for return," and that is the last we see of the information. That is hardly a courteous way in which to treat hon. members of this House in regard to matters concerning an important department.

Will my hon.
friend let me know, if he can, any particular return he desires in reference to the militia estimates?

The minister has
sufficient officials in his department to look after these returns. Some time ago, I started to make up a list of them, and I found many that had been entirely disregarded. The secretary of the department is, I assume, the official to whom these matters go. Is the House to understand that when orders for returns are issued, they are not to be obeyed at all, and that when the question is brought up, we are to be asked what particular one we want before the others. We want them all, and that is what we are entitled to have.

The questions
that have been asked of the Department of Militia and Defence are perhaps as numerous as those asked of all the other departments put together, and the information asked for has been forthcoming with the greatest possible celerity. There are a few returns that are not yet ready but that will be ready shortly. I placed a return on the table of the House to-day, and I
shall be able to place several more on the Table to-morrow. My hon. friend is not right in stating that no returns that have been asked for have been laid upon the Table.
Will the minister give the dates?
I cannot give the exact day or month, any more than my hon. friend is able to give the information asked of him; but there have been returns laid on the table of the House.
Not since we met after the adjournment in February.
I am under the impression that not a single return which has any reference to the militia estimates and which has been asked for, has not been laid on the table of the House. *

The minister will recall that it was distinctly understood that, in order to facilitate the departure of the Prime Minister in February, when the militia estimates came up, any matters in reference to the appropriations for the war could be discussed. I assume that the minister is aware of that. How many officers in uniform are employed in and around the Militia. Department on staff and other duties?

The officers on
the Headquarters Staff are the Inspector General of Canada, Quartermaster General, Chief of General Staff, Adjutant General, Master General of Ordnance, Judge Advocate General, Director General Engineer Services, Director General of Mobilization, a Director General Medical Services, Director General Supplies and Transport, Director General Clothing and Equipment, Director General, of Musketry, Assistant Adjutant General (2),-Assistant Adjutant General (1), Military Secretary, Director of Artillery, Director of Stores, Chief Inspector of Small Arms, Director General Works and Buildings, Director of Military Training, Assistant Paymaster General, Director of Military Operations, Assistant Director of Supplies and Transport, Officer for Imperial Staff at War Officer, a/Offioer i/o Stores Audit, Deputy Assistant Adjutant General, Assistant Director Engineers Services, Assistant Director Military Intelligence, Assistant Director Military Surveys, Assistant Director of Signalling, Chief Instructor of Musketry, Staff Office to Inspector General.
And the non-commissioned officers?
About 175 military clerks and 75 orderly clerks.

Are these men on
service pay?
They are paid according to their rank in the militia. They form part of the Permanent Force and receive the allowance paid to members of the Permanent Force.
They are not really in the Civil Service, hut are treated as on active service and are paid accordingly?
Yes.
How many of them are returned soldiers?

I cannot give the exact number, but it has been our policy to employ as many returned soldiers as possible. Whenever a vacancy occurs we seek out a returned soldier. A great many of the men on the staff are not physically fit fox overseas service.
Perhaps the minister would let me know how many of them axe returned soldiers when his estimates are up again. [DOT]
I shall be glad to.
Will the minister also inform me when next his estimates are up, how many men are employed at Halifax on the Headquarters Medical Staff, and everything of that nature?
I shall get that information for my hon. friend.

In the county of Cape Breton we have very large coal, iron and steel industries, all contributing essentially to the production of munitions in this country. Right at the coal
11	p.m. mines is the landing place of one of the Atlantic cables, and on account of that it has been necessary to have a home guard regiment right in the town of North Sydney and at Sydney Mines. It has done excellent work, and has been instrumental in maintaining good order in that vicinity. A large number of foreigners are employed at these mines and steel works, and I have reason to believe that we might have difficulty with these men if the regiment were not stationed there all the time. That is one of the chief reasons why the 94th Regiment has been kept there. That regiment has also been an excellent medium for sending men to the front, over 600 men and some excellent

officers having gone forward from time to time. There is quite a large number of this regiment left, some at Louisburg, some at Glace Bay, some at North Sydney and some at Sydney Mines, defending the Marconi towers and other works. What I wish to bring particularly to the attention of the .minister is that these men are complaining of the pay they receive. Many of them are heads of families and are getting only $1.10 a day. These men are doing a good service for their country, although they are not at the front, and it is almost impossible for a *man to support his family on $1.10 a day. in view of the present cost of foodstuffs. I think the minister should take this into consideration and endeavour to get better pay for these men, who are rendering excellent service to their country.
All they get is $1.10 a day?
That is all they get.
They get subsistence allowance as well.
Married men get $1.10 a day and 45 cents subsistence allowance.
Even that is small pay under present conditions.
Yes, it is.

I wish to draw the attention of the minister to* a matter concerning the pay of the men enlisted in the Forestry battalions. I understand that special pay has been given to men with special qualifications in these battalions, such as sawyers, imiillwrigfhts, saw filers and so on. They enlist as privates, but if they are doing sawmill work or expert forestry work they receive extra pay. I believe the rates of pay are as follows:

They are promised this pay when they enlist in these Forestry battalions, but once they draw this pay the Patriotic Fund is cut off from their wives an.d families. Is that action taken by the Militia Department or is it by the local organization of the Patriotic Fund.

I cannot speak
as to the correctness of my hon. friend's

figures, but I have no doubt that what he says is right. Extra pay is given to certain classes of experts 'who join the Forestry battalions such as isaw filers and those whom my bon. friend has named.. He states that for that reason the administration of the Patriotic Fund withhold the allowance and give it to those who do. not get that extra pay. The Government have nothing to do with the administration of the Patriotic Fund. It is a voluntary organization and I could not speak with authority as to what the Patriotic Fund Association do. with regard to withholding the allowance from the few men- who get extra wages.

The minister must
recognize that some action must be taken by the Militia Department or the Patriotic Fund administration would not know that these men get this extra pay.

Any information
in regard to the families of soldiers is readily given to the Patriotic Association by the department and vice versa.

The claim made in regard to this special work of the Forestry battalions is that these men have more arduous duties than the ordinary private or non-commissioned officer. Their hours are longer anid they are called upon to do much more expert and arduous work than the private soldier getting $1.10 a day with separation and Patriotic Fund allowances. Quite a number of complaints have come from men who have been induced to. enter these Forestry battalions on the understanding that, on .account of the expert nature of the work, they would get .added pay. When they found that the Patriotic Fund allowance was withheld from their wives and families they naturally felt aggrieved. I quite understand that the department has nothing to do with the administration of the Patriotic Fund but if these men were induced to enlist under false pretenses I do not think the department can shirk the responsibility.

I am one of the Central
Executive of the Patriotic Fund and the proceedings are along this line: various standard allowances in different parts of Canada were determined upon as being such as to meet the requirements for reasonable subsistence. The men who received special pay in Forestry battalions were required to show what this amount was and if the total amount that they were receiving with respect to the work they were doing did not exceed what was considered a reasonable subsistence allowance the Patriotic Fund supplemented the money that the men were receiving, hut if they were earning in connection with their work an amount which equalled a reasonable .subsistence allowance the Patriotic Fund did not contribute. Whether or not there was any misrepresentation I cannot say, but it has been well understood for some time that no Patriotic Fund money would be paid where men were receiving more than what was reasonably necessary for subsistence.

I would like to point out in this connection that there is quite clearly a misrepresentation to the men. A man is engaged .as a .sawyer. He is to get extra pay but if the patriotic .allowance upon which he depended for his family is cut off then there is misrepresentation to him for which the Militia Department will have to be held responsible. I hope this Parliament will not agree to a juggling between the Patriotic Fund and the Militia Department to deprive a man who has enlisted in good faith to render special services of the allowance that he had every reason to believe be would get upon his joining. If he renders the service he is entitled to the pay. This is an agreement between the man who enlists and the .authorities and that agreement should be carried out.

How much was each
man promised by the Patriotic Fund?
I do not know.
Of course not; it would be impossible to answer that.

It is not impossible to
answer but I do not happen to he familiar with the grant. Unless the Patriotic Fund is considered to be an established grant supplementing the separation allowance there is a misunderstanding in regard to the Tights of those who enlist. That being the case, the man enlists on the understanding that his family is going to get so much separation allowance and so much from the Patriotio Fund.
No.

My hon. friend has not enlisted. That is the understanding of those who enlist, and they have the right when they enlist to have that understating. If those who control the Patriotic Fund say that is not the understanding then I say they are juggling with the men and are not treating them fairly. If the Militia Department is a party to that transaction

it is not doing its duty towards these men and it is not doing the country any credit.

For special service, such as forestry work, inducements are held out to expert men to join on the understanding that they will get this added pay and their separation allowance as well as participation in the Patriotic Fund. I have seen dozen of appeals made to men in Edmonton asking them to join and holding out this inducement to them. These men leave expecting that their wives and families will benefit toy this fund but after they get to England they find that the allowance is cut off. Sometimes they do not know it for months. I quite concur in what my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) says-these men are enlisted under false pretenses. 1 do not know whethe1" the Militia Department is to blame, but I think there has been a misunderstanding and if so the matter should be righted.

I do not recollect having seen any complaints from any. of the thousands of men enlisted in the forestry battalions in regard to this matter. My officers do not remember having received a complaint. I do not doubt that my hon. friend is correct in his statement, but no complaint has come to the attention of the department, so far as I know. The assigned pay, separation allowance and pay of a soldier are matters for which the Government is responsible. The Patriotic Fund is a voluntary organization whose practice is to supplement the pay and allowance given to the families. I am informed it is extended only to those who need a supplementary allowance, and in proportion to their needs. No soldier's family that did not need this extra allowance would make: a claim upon the Patriotic Association. If they did, they should not get an allowance.

The minister knows that a complaint is not likely to be made by a private soldier, under military rules. The position of the Patriotic Fund is, of course, as the minister states, but the fact remains that these recruiting officers induced men to join under false pretenses by giving them to understand that if they joined the Forestry battalions as experts they were to get $2.25 per day, and their wives and children were to receive the allowance from the Patriotic Fund in addition.
Who is to judge of the needs of the man and his family?
The local branch of the Patriotic Fund Association who are in a position to ascertain the condition of each family.

Surely the best judge of the needs of the family is the man himself, and if he enlists on the understand ing that he is to receive certain extra pay, surely that understanding should be lived up to. It is not creditable to either the Patriotic Association or the Government that there should be any juggling between the Government and the Patriotic Association to mislead a man and deprive him of what he believed was to be given to him.

The only attempted juggling in connection with this matter has been on the part of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mt. Oliver). Although he has kept himself in splendid practice along that line for some weeks or months past, he has made :a mighty poor fist of his attempt at, it to-night. He knows and the .people know that the Government has nothing whatever to do with, the Patriotic Fund. A recruiting agent asks a -man. to enlist. He Jjas a. right to tell that man that 'he will get certain .pay from the Government and a certain separation allowance, a definite amount. He may tell the man that, even though he might be in a forestry battalion, he .would have a claim on the Patriotic Fund if his necessities required it. That was all. But in regard to that, or any other statement of the kind, the Government is not responsible. The fund is .administered through the local boards in the different counties. In my county of Fron-.tenae the beeve of each township, is the man who will best know the rights of any case where .a call is made on the fund. Some families will get a certain amount per month, others in the same township will

get twice as much, because their need is twice as great. The fund has been long enough in existence to have people understand that it is administered quite independently of the Government. The Department of Militia has nothing whatever to do with it. I think it is entirely useless fox the hon. gentleman, from Edmonton to try to make out -that the department is responsible fox it.

I will make another attempt. It is a fact that the agent of the department secures the enlistment of the men. It is on the representations made by the agent of the department that the man enlists. This man enlists, not as a matter of charity, but as a matter of business. These men are experts and enlist for pay, as well as for the benefit of their country. They are given definitely to understand that they are to receive pay because of their expert ability, and after they have enlisted, according to the statement made by the hon. gentleman from Kingston, the Patriotic Fund Association goes into the matter and if this man's extra pay is greater than the allowance his family would receive from the Patriotic Fund, liis family does not get anything from the Patriotic Fund, and he, therefore, does not get any allowance whatever for his expert ability which the Government is getting the benefit of, and which they hired him for the purpose of getting the benefit of.

I made myself anything but clear, if my hon. friend so understood m-e. What I endeavoured to say was this: in each district throughout 'Canada there is a>
determination by the Patriotic Fund as to what amount is reasonably necessary to meet living expenses. If a man enters into a contract with the Government for special pay from the Government, in addition to his military pay and allowances, he gets that special pay. The contract with the Government is respected in every detail, but if the amount he receives from the Government, as special pay or otherwise, is in excess of the amount that is decided throughout Canada as being reasonable by the Patriotic Fund for subsistence in each district, then the Patriotic Fund does not supplement in any way what the Government gives, but it has no power to take, nor does it intend to take, anything from what the Government has directed to give the man.
It comes exactly to what I said.
Not at all.
That the expert man in a Forestry battalion in the end gets no more than the man who is not an expert.
Not at all.
That is absolutely the hon. gentleman's calculation, and that is the complaint my hon. friend (Mr. Douglas) makes.

The Patriotic Fund might give to a wife and family $10 a month in excess of ordinary pay. Take a private getting $1.10 a day and $20 separation allowance, if the man got $3 a day extra, that would be $90 a month; the Patriotic Fund could not deprive him of any p^rt of that $90. He would still get his military pay and allowance, and the extra $3. I am taking that as an illustration. They can in no way take from him what the Government directs that he should receive. They would simply say, "You are getting more than the Patriotic Fund was granting to those similarly situated," but the Patriotic Fund will not supplement the amount. The man might get more from the Patriotic Fund in certain circumstances than the other man.
He might and might not.
It depends on the obligations.

But the principle is that the man who enlists for special pay, so far as the Dominion Government is concerned, is deprived of that extra pay by reason of the withdrawal of the Patriotic Fund, and the man who has no expert knowledge, as far as that is concerned, stands on an equality with the man who has expert knowledge. If the Government had no knowledge of that before, they have knowledge of it now, and if they have no co-operation with the Patriotic Fund, I say, for the sake of their own good faith, they should co-operate with it in that matter, and the authorities of the Patriotic Fund should know that they did make such and such a bargain with this man, and that the necessities of a family are to be governed by that bargain, and not by the views of the officers of the Patriotic Fund, who apparently pay no regard to the direction that has been made.

I know a case in point, bearing out what the hon. gentleman has said, of a man who enlisted, who had a wife and two children. Before he became a log setter he was getting $1.10 a day,

which is $34.10 a month, $22 a month from the Patriotic Fund, and $20 separation allowance, making $76.10 a month. With the extra pay he got at the rate of $1.75 a day, his pay came to $54.25, separation allowance $20, which gave him $74.25 per month, and he actually was getting less as an expert than he was getting as a private soldier drawing pay from the Patriotic Fund.

I think it will be very desirable if any member with knowledge of such facts would draw the attention of the Patriotic Fund Association to them. That is an immense organization which does a great deal of good, and they are not trying to shirk their responsibility at all. They desire to act fairly with every family. I would ask my hon. friend, if at any time he has a family in mind, who, he thinks, are not being paid, to bring the matter to the attention of the hon. secretary of the association, Sir Herbert Ames, who sits in this House, or any officer of the association, and they will be very sympathetic in the matter.

Sometimes men do not care to go to the Patriotic Fund and state that their family requires the money. Here is a man who left a wife and two children and they are drawing $74.25. That is pretty fair remuneration, but that is not the point. He joined on the understanding that, as an expert log setter, he would get $1.75 a day and $20 a month separation allowance, and that his wife would participate in the Patriotic Fund, which he does not look upon as a charity at all, but simply as a part of his pay-he has been given to understand that in our province at least, I do not know what has happened in other sections. In our province, the Patriotic Fund money has been held, out as an inducement, just in the same way as the pay and separation allowance has been held out, and he has been induced to enlist on that understanding, and he does not consider he is getting any charity when he is drawing $22 a month for his wife and two children from the Patriotic Fund.

I wish to call to the notice of the minister, in view of the discussion we had about those different allowances, that in the case which I brought to his notice the man does not get anything from the Patriotic Fund or from the Red Cross for separation allowance.
They get an allowance in lieu of separation allowance.

I was not aware of
that. The minister did not answer my request on behalf of these men, and I hope that, either now or when the matter comes up again, he will promise to give some consideration to it. It has been brought to my notice, and I should have brought it up in the House long ago, but was waiting for this opportunity to do so. I wish to impress upon the minister that the moneys these men get are not enough to support their family and themselves under present conditions.

If the minister would pass all but one item on this page with which we are now dealing, and adjourn-
'Sir EDWARD KEMP: I sympathize with my hon. friend in his request. I may say we tried to proceed on Friday last, and my hon. friend from Pictou asked to let the Estimates stand, a:Sd we got on late this evening. We could leave one item open, so that we could discuss any matter.
I was assuming my hon, friend is coming back to-morrow.
Yes.

There are certain
explanations we must get to-morrow. T was only suggesting we should adjourn.
My suggestion is that we leave one item on page 49 upon which we may later discuss anything.

How many officers have we now in Canada in charge o>f the work of securing recruits for home defence, how much money is that work costing per day, :and how many recruits have been secured through the efforts of those officers during the past 'month? A gentleman placed a case before one the other day; whether it was imaginary or real I should not like to say, but I think 'that there was some realism in it. He said that .a widow came to him who had $100 which she wished to invest in a wax savings certificate. She 'asked this gentleman, who was a friend of hers, what the Government would do with her $100. Well, he said, Colonel So-and-So will get $12 of it, Major So-and-So gets $8, Captain So-and-So a further amount-he gave a list of the names. He found that without going outside a radius of about five miles, the old lady's entire $100 would be taken up in allowances to officers who, to all appearances, were not doing any work; they were 'attending to their ordinary business every day. If that be the

case, my (hon. friend has a chance to effect a great economy in that direction.
The Kingston Whig charges that 'two- officers in Kingston-their names, df I remember correctly, were Brown and Wilson-are being retired to make way for political friends of the Government. Will the minister be prepared to give us a statement tomorrow with regard to this? I think the suggestion is reasonable that we .pass one or two items .and leave the rest. We will pass the first two items.

The officers of the Canadian Defence Force are also employe^ for the purpose of recruiting in .the Canadian Expeditionary Force, -and have done a good service. Some men who -enlisted in the Canadian Defence Force have gone over to the Canadian Expeditionary Force. These officers are toeing gradually let out. After to-morrow none of them will toe getting pay.

This gentleman was
probably right, then.

Sometimes there is an impression that because a man in uniform does not work with his hands, he is not doing anything. As to the officers at Kingston, I saw that item in the paper. There is absolutely no politics in the matter at all; the article is incorrect in more ways than one. A number of officers throughout the country are being let out now. Both officers to whom my hon. friend refers are employees of the Inland Revenue Department and have been drawing their full salaries from that department with military pay since the early days of the war. The services of quite -a few officers in different parts of the country are not needed now as much as they have been hitherto in the work of recruiting. We are trying to economize, and at the same time we are trying to act fairly to those men. They have done what the country has asked them to do, and if those whose profession was not that of soldier before the war toegan can secure employment now-they have better opportunity of doing that at the present time than they would be likely to have when demobilization is taking place after peace is declared-it is just as well for them to take that into consideration.
These officers in Kingston are not going to be replaced by other officers to do the same work?
It is a matter of reducing the staff; we are doing it all over the country.

Will the minister let me know to-morrow whether the contracts for certain supplies for the Langara and Braemar Military Hospitals in British Columbia, tenders for which closed on June 6, have been awarded?
That comes under the Military Hospitals Commission, of which Sir James Lougheed is the chairman.
If it has relation to a military hospital attached to some unit, it wi-ll come under the Department of Militia.	.

I shall be very glad to look it up, in any case.
Progress reported.
